evidence.snippet: In two unrelated families, a heterozygous missense mutation, c.632C-->T (p.A211V), was found to segregate with DFNA25 deafness and was not present in 267 controls.
evidence.explanation: The founding allele, its zygosity, its segregation and its control screening.

evidence.snippet: The A211 residue is conserved in VGLUT3 across species and in all human VGLUT subtypes (VGLUT1-3), suggesting an important functional role.
evidence.explanation: The conservation argument the founding paper rests the missense call on.

evidence.snippet: The novel frameshift mutation, p.M206Nfs*4, in which methionine is changed to asparagine at amino acid position 206, resulted in a termination codon at amino acid position 209.
evidence.explanation: The 2016 report identified a frameshift in one sequenced proband and predicted truncation; it did not show cosegregation in all affected relatives.

evidence.snippet: A novel splicing mutation, c.763+1G>T, in the solute carrier family 17, member 8 (SLC17A8) gene was identified in the patients, and the genotypes of the mutation were co-segregated with the phenotype of HL.
evidence.explanation: The splice-donor allele and its co-segregation in a three-generation dominant family.

steps/1.description: The founding c.632C>T (p.A211V) variant segregated in two families with evidence of distant shared ancestry and was absent from 267 controls. Later reports include c.616dupA (p.M206Nfs*4) and c.763+1G>T. The 2016 frameshift report sequenced one proband from an affected pedigree; it did not demonstrate segregation across all eight affected relatives. Predicted truncation and splice disruption do not establish a shared dominant mechanism.

evidence.snippet: In the cochlea, VGLUT3 accumulates glutamate in the synaptic vesicles of the sensory inner hair cells (IHCs) before releasing it onto receptors of auditory-nerve terminals.
evidence.explanation: The normal function of the protein, which is what the disease removes or alters.

evidence.snippet: among its isoforms (VGLUT1-3), only VGLUT3 is expressed selectively in the inner hair cells (IHCs)
evidence.explanation: Inner hair cell expression provides a basis for nonredundant cochlear function. It does not explain the absence of extra-auditory findings in every carrier.

evidence.snippet: This variation does not impair the glutamate vesicular accumulation, neither the quantal release nor the quantal content in hippocampal autaptic neurons
evidence.explanation: A negative result at the level of transport itself, which is why this entry does not assert that the human missense allele simply stops glutamate loading. Graded IN_VITRO because the measurement is in cultured autaptic neurons.

evidence.snippet: the p.A224V variant does not disturb the VGLUT3 targeting within the hair cell cytoplasm.
evidence.explanation: Semi-quantitative mouse cochlear immunofluorescence; this limits extrapolation from reduced central-terminal expression.

steps/2.description: VGLUT3 supports glutamate loading into inner hair cell synaptic vesicles. Null mice lack functional auditory afferent transmission, but human A211V does not abolish uptake or quantal signaling in tested heterologous/autaptic preparations. Central-terminal protein reduction in the knock-in cannot be assumed in cochlear cells: the 2021 study found comparable inner hair cell VGLUT3 immunofluorescence and distribution between genotypes. Variant-specific effects therefore remain important.

evidence.snippet: We now report that mice lacking VGLUT3 are profoundly deaf due to the absence of glutamate release from hair cells at the first synapse in the auditory pathway.
evidence.explanation: The release failure stated directly, and its location at the first auditory synapse.

evidence.snippet: Ca(2+)-triggered synaptic-vesicle turnover was normal in IHCs of Slc17a8 null mice when probed by membrane capacitance measurements at 2 weeks of age.
evidence.explanation: The deliberate negative result that localises the defect to vesicle content rather than to exocytosis. Without it the node would be indistinguishable from a fusion defect.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that deafness in Slc17a8-deficient mice is due to a specific defect of vesicular glutamate uptake and release and that VGLUT3 is essential for auditory coding at the IHC synapse.
evidence.explanation: The founding paper's own conclusion about the null animal.

steps/3.description: In the Ruel Slc17a8-null line, calcium-triggered vesicle turnover was preserved at two weeks and surviving ribbons had a normal ultrastructural appearance at three months, while auditory afferent signaling failed. Other null-model studies reported thin or elongated ribbons. The findings differ by study and preparation; they do not establish universally normal ribbon morphology or uniform transport loss in dominant human variants.

evidence.snippet: Scanning electron microscopy examinations demonstrated the collapse of stereocilia bundles in IHCs, leaving those from outer hair cells unaffected.
evidence.explanation: The bundle finding and its restriction to inner hair cells.

steps/4.description: Homozygous A224V mice show progressive inner hair cell bundle fusion and collapse with relative preservation of outer hair cell bundles. VGLUT3 is not localized to stereocilia, and the molecular connection is unresolved. Protein misfolding/trafficking effects and interaction with the C57BL/6J Cdh23 background are hypotheses. Comparable inner hair cell immunofluorescence argues against gross protein accumulation but cannot exclude altered turnover or proteostasis.

evidence.snippet: The summating potential was reduced, indicating the alteration of inner hair cell (IHC) receptor potential.
evidence.explanation: The measurement and the authors' own interpretation of it.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that DFNA25 stems from a failure in the mechano-transduction followed by a change in synaptic transfer.
evidence.explanation: The ordering claim that this hypothesis group is built on, stated by the authors as a suggestion rather than a demonstration - which is why the group is EMERGING.

steps/5.description: The summating potential is the gross cochlear correlate of the inner hair cell receptor potential, and it is reduced in the knock-in mouse. Because cochlear amplification is intact in the same animals, a smaller receptor potential is being generated from a normal mechanical input - which is what a transduction defect in the inner hair cell looks like from outside.

evidence.snippet: However, synaptic ribbons became abnormally elongated in knock‐in mice
evidence.explanation: Mouse cochlear imaging supports ribbon enlargement, not a measured increase in glutamate secretion.

steps/6.description: Homozygous A224V inner hair cell ribbons enlarge markedly at four to six months, with preserved ribbon and synapse counts in the sampled region. This structural change follows early bundle abnormalities. Its causal contribution to hearing loss, including whether it is compensatory, remains unresolved.

evidence.snippet: patch-clamp membrane capacitance measurements showed an increase in the rate of the sustained releasable pool exocytosis
evidence.explanation: Ex-vivo patch-clamp measurements in isolated mouse organs of Corti; membrane fusion does not determine glutamate quantal content.

steps/7.description: At six months, freshly dissected homozygous A224V inner hair cells show increased sustained exocytic capacitance responses to long depolarizations, with preserved calcium currents and readily releasable pool responses. Capacitance measures membrane fusion rather than vesicular glutamate content or afferent neurotransmission. The change may reflect compensation or extrasynaptic release; it is not established as a cause of hearing loss.

evidence.snippet: Null mice with a targeted deletion of Slc17a8 exon 2 lacked auditory-nerve responses to acoustic stimuli, although auditory brainstem responses could be elicited by electrical stimuli, and robust otoacoustic emissions were recorded.
evidence.explanation: All three halves of the dissociation in one sentence: no acoustic neural response, preserved electrical response, preserved emissions.

evidence.snippet: Using auditory brainstem response and distortion product otoacoustic emissions, we showed progressive hearing loss with intact cochlear amplification in the VGLUT3A224V/A224V mouse.
evidence.explanation: The same dissociation in the allele-matched model, and in progressive rather than congenital form.

steps/8.description: Slc17a8-null mice lack sound-evoked auditory responses while retaining otoacoustic emissions and electrically evoked brainstem responses. Homozygous A224V mice show progressive auditory threshold elevation with preserved emissions. Human otoacoustic-emission data are sparse and differ from these model findings; this node records experimental physiology rather than a universal human diagnostic signature.

evidence.snippet: Later, the number of afferent synapses, spiral ganglion neurons, and lateral efferent endings below sensory IHCs declined.
evidence.explanation: The deafferentation itself, and its late timing relative to the functional deficit.

evidence.snippet: The early degeneration of some cochlear ganglion neurons in knockout mice also indicates an important developmental role for the glutamate released by hair cells before the onset of hearing.
evidence.explanation: The developmental component, which is a different claim from use-dependent loss and is the reason a congenital null and an adult-onset human disease may diverge here.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we analyzed the cochlear structure of aged Vglut3KO mice, revealing significant degeneration of inner hair cells, synapses, and stereocilia.
evidence.explanation: The structural endpoint in the aged null animal.

steps/9.description: Null mice show loss of afferent synapses, spiral ganglion neurons and lateral efferent endings; some neuronal loss precedes hearing onset. Older null cochleae also show inner hair cell and stereocilia degeneration. These observations raise questions about treatment timing, but do not define a human therapeutic window. Rescue studies in post-neonatal null mice remain distinct from dominant human disease.

evidence.snippet: we identified a novel dominant locus, DFNA25, for delayed-onset, progressive, high-frequency, nonsyndromic sensorineural hearing loss in a large, multigenerational United States family of Czech descent.
evidence.explanation: The phenotype as defined at the locus, in the founding kindred.

evidence.snippet: We have identified SLC17A8, which encodes the vesicular glutamate transporter-3 (VGLUT3), as the gene responsible for DFNA25, an autosomal-dominant form of progressive, high-frequency nonsyndromic deafness.
evidence.explanation: The same phenotype restated once the gene was in hand.

steps/10.description: Progressive, predominantly high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss is the characteristic presentation in the founding families. Audiogram shape and severity vary. Family-based ascertainment and a dated ClinGen proband count do not support a population-wide phenotype frequency.

edges/1.description: Every proposed mechanism for this disease runs through the transporter that the variant sits in.

edges/2.description: The direct consequence of an unfilled vesicle, and the route the null mouse takes.

edges/3.description: The route the allele-matched knock-in mouse takes. It is marked INDIRECT because no mechanism connecting an altered vesicular transporter to hair-bundle architecture has been demonstrated; the knock-in shows the bundles collapse, not why.

evidence.snippet: In addition, IHC ribbon synapses underwent structural and functional modifications at later stages.
evidence.explanation: The genotype-associated synaptic findings do not prove that reduced receptor potential caused them.

edges/4.description: The A224V genotype is associated with this later synaptic alteration; the intermediates and relationship to the early bundle defect remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: patch-clamp membrane capacitance measurements showed an increase in the rate of the sustained releasable pool exocytosis
evidence.explanation: The genotype-associated synaptic findings do not prove that reduced receptor potential caused them.

edges/5.description: The A224V genotype is associated with this later synaptic alteration; the intermediates and relationship to the early bundle defect remain unresolved.

edges/6.description: An afferent terminal that receives no transmitter does not fire, however well the cochlea in front of it is working.

edges/7.description: Bundle disruption and reduced summating potential support a mechanotransduction defect in the same homozygous model; direct mechanotransducer-current impairment was not measured.

edges/8.description: Reduced inner hair cell receptor potential is proposed to reduce afferent drive. The model shows reduced summating and compound action potentials, but does not directly quantify sound-evoked glutamate release.

edges/9.description: Loss of afferent signaling and later deafferentation occur in null mice; glutamate also has developmental effects, so this is not established as a direct use-dependent degeneration mechanism in humans.

edges/10.description: Impaired afferent sound encoding provides a model-based explanation for hearing loss. The progressive human course is not reproduced by the congenitally deaf null model.

edges/11.description: Reduced afferent innervation may contribute to sustained hearing impairment in null models; its contribution and reversibility in human DFNA25 are unknown.

evidence.snippet: Variants in this gene segregated with disease in 28 additional members in two families
evidence.explanation: The segregation evidence behind the Definitive classification.

evidence.snippet: In summary, SCL17A8 is definitively associated with autosomal dominant nonsyndromic hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: The panel's summary sentence. The gene symbol is transposed in the source record and is quoted as written.

genes/0.notes: SLC17A8 encodes VGLUT3. ClinGen classified its dominant nonsyndromic hearing loss relationship as Definitive in 2023; the counted probands and variants describe that assessment. A211V, c.616dupA and c.763+1G>T differ in their supporting segregation and functional evidence. The 2016 frameshift was found in one sequenced proband with an affected pedigree; the splice report demonstrated cosegregation, but did not establish transcript consequences in its abstract. The 2021 cell study tested the already reported c.616dupA alongside c.824C>A, rather than discovering two additional alleles.

evidence.snippet: customized by an audiologist to the degree and frequency of hearing loss, can be used in individuals with mild-to-severe hearing loss.
evidence.explanation: General hearing-aid guidance, not a DFNA25 outcome estimate.

treatments/0.description: Offer audiologist-fitted amplification and communication support according to hearing thresholds, speech testing and individual preferences. This follows general genetic hearing-loss care; genotype-specific benefit cannot be predicted from the null mouse or an isolated OAE finding.

evidence.snippet: Habilitation for hearing loss includes improved access to sound through hearing aids or cochlear implants
evidence.explanation: General habilitation options; no SLC17A8-specific outcome is asserted.

treatments/1.description: Consider cochlear implantation under standard audiologic candidacy assessment when amplification provides insufficient benefit. Preserved electrically evoked responses in null mice provide mechanistic plausibility, but do not establish human DFNA25 implant efficacy or guarantee preservation of the neural target.

evidence.snippet: although auditory brainstem responses could be elicited by electrical stimuli
evidence.explanation: The preserved electrical responsiveness that an implant would exploit. Model evidence for a human intervention, so the claim in the description is plausibility rather than efficacy.

treatments/1/targets/0.description: Direct electrical stimulation of the spiral ganglion substitutes for the defective inner hair cell synapse.

evidence.snippet: These findings represent a successful restoration of hearing by gene replacement in mice, which is a significant advance toward gene therapy of human deafness.
evidence.explanation: The authors' own framing of how far the result reaches - toward human therapy, not to it.

evidence.snippet: rescued hearing in adult deaf Slc17A8 −/− mice by restoring VGLUT3 protein expression in inner hair cells
evidence.explanation: Primary 2023 adult-null-mouse rescue supporting the CSF-delivery theme in the research report.

treatments/2.description: Preclinical gene replacement has restored auditory responses in homozygous null mice after neonatal cochlear AAV1 delivery, adult intracisternal delivery through the cochlear aqueduct, and AAV8 injection at five weeks with assessment 27 weeks later. The latter does not demonstrate reversal after treatment of already aged animals. These interventions have not established efficacy in dominant A211V disease; augmentation, suppression or combined strategies require variant-specific testing. No human SLC17A8 interventional study was identified in the reviewed research; the registered NCT01802190 study is observational.

evidence.snippet: Within 2 weeks of AAV1-VGLUT3 delivery, auditory brainstem response (ABR) thresholds normalize, along with partial rescue of the startle response.
evidence.explanation: The functional rescue, in the null mouse.

evidence.snippet: Auditory brainstem response (ABR) testing demonstrated restoration of auditory function following gene therapy.
evidence.explanation: Mice were injected at five weeks and evaluated 27 weeks later, so the aged endpoint does not establish efficacy when treatment starts in aged animals.

treatments/2/targets/0.description: Restoring VGLUT3 protein to the inner hair cell addresses the molecular lesion rather than its consequences - in an animal that has none of the protein to begin with.

evidence.snippet: Regular follow up is recommended for all individuals with genetic hearing loss
evidence.explanation: General surveillance baseline.

evidence.snippet: persons with documented hearing loss should be counseled appropriately and repeated overexposure to loud noises should be avoided.
evidence.explanation: General precaution; no demonstrated DFNA25-specific disease-modifying effect.

treatments/3.description: Follow hearing serially and adjust rehabilitation as needed. Avoid repeated loud-noise overexposure using general hearing-loss guidance. No SLC17A8-specific surveillance interval or proven genotype-specific noise susceptibility is inferred.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with autosomal dominant hearing loss have a 50% chance of transmitting the pathogenic variant to each child.
evidence.explanation: General autosomal dominant transmission probability, distinct from penetrance.

evidence.snippet: Once the pathogenic variant(s) have been identified in the family, prenatal and preimplantation genetic testing for genetic hearing loss are possible.
evidence.explanation: General reproductive-testing guidance after identification of the familial variant.

treatments/4.description: Discuss 50% variant transmission per pregnancy, variable onset and penetrance, familial testing and reproductive options. Counseling should respect individual communication and reproductive preferences.

hypotheses/0.description: VGLUT3 deficiency prevents vesicular glutamate loading and auditory afferent activation in homozygous null mice despite preserved vesicle fusion and cochlear amplification. This is an established null-model mechanism and a candidate contributor to human SLC17A8 disease. It does not establish haploinsufficiency or uniform transport loss for dominant variants: A211V retains transport in tested heterologous systems, and human onset and severity vary.

hypotheses/1.description: Homozygous A224V mice develop inner hair cell stereocilia disruption and reduced summating potentials before marked ribbon enlargement and increased sustained exocytosis. This supports a mechanotransduction-first hypothesis in that model. Temporal order does not establish that the bundle lesion causes the synaptic changes, and the dominant human mechanism remains unconfirmed.

open_questions/0.rationale: Homozygous knock-in mice have progressive impairment but heterozygotes have only mild changes over six months. Lifespan, allele dose, genetic background and species-specific biology may contribute. Null rescue does not select the optimal strategy for dominant human alleles.

open_questions/1.rationale: The detailed primary human observation concerns one proband, while both main mouse models retain emissions. Broader human OAE, cochlear microphonic, ABR, age and exposure data are needed to separate cochlear and neural contributions. Controlled mouse noise experiments can test model susceptibility but cannot establish the cause of human findings.

open_questions/2.rationale: A224V mice show bundle collapse despite retained transport in heterologous systems and comparable cochlear VGLUT3 immunofluorescence. Proteostasis, trafficking and the Cdh23 background remain candidate contributors. Identifying the mechanism could guide therapy, but a gene-directed intervention might affect both bundle and synaptic consequences.

open_questions/3.rationale: Missense, frameshift and splice alleles have unequal human and functional evidence. The frameshift and c.824C>A expression study retested reported alleles. Allelic heterogeneity does not by itself justify splitting a disease, and a normal heterozygous-null mouse does not resolve the human dominant mechanism.

evidence.snippet: ARCI is caused by biallelic mutations in ABCA12, ALOX12B, ALOXE3, CERS3, CYP4F22, NIPAL4, PNPLA1, SDR9C7, SULT2B1, and TGM1.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports the core biallelic ARCI gene spectrum.

evidence.snippet: DNA was extracted from peripheral blood and analyzed for the 13 described ARCI genes-TGM1, ABCA12, ALOX12B, ALOXE3, CERS3, CYP4F22, LIPN, NIPAL4, PNPLA1, SDR9C7, SLC27A4, SULT2B1, and CASP14 by next-generation sequencing using an in-house panel.
evidence.explanation: Extends the gene set of this node beyond the ten-gene list above to the thirteen genes screened on contemporary non-syndromic ARCI panels, which is where LIPN and CASP14 come from. Graded BACKGROUND because the gene list is prior knowledge the study restates in its methods.

steps/12.description: ARCI begins with biallelic pathogenic variants in a heterogeneous set of genes involved in epidermal cornification, lipid transport, lipid metabolism, and filaggrin catabolism.

evidence.snippet: The mean ichthyosis severity score in TGM1- and ABCA12-mutated patients was significantly higher than in all other mutated genes, while the lowest score was observed in CYP4F22-mutated patients.
evidence.explanation: Supports TGM1 as a high-severity ARCI genotype.

evidence.snippet: Ultrastructural data available for 56 patients showed a 100% specificity of cholesterol clefts for TGM1-mutated cases and revealed abnormal lamellar bodies in SDR9C7 and CERS3 patients.
evidence.explanation: Supports a genotype-informative ultrastructural abnormality in TGM1-associated ARCI.

steps/13.description: TGM1-associated ARCI disrupts transglutaminase-dependent cornified-envelope formation in differentiating keratinocytes; this mechanism is associated with higher severity and thick brownish scales in cohort data.

evidence.snippet: Loss-of-function mutations on both alleles generally result in harlequin ichthyosis, whereas biallelic missense mutations mainly lead to CIE or LI.
evidence.explanation: Supports ABCA12 functional severity as a determinant of the ARCI phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Ultrastructural data available for 56 patients showed a 100% specificity of cholesterol clefts for TGM1-mutated cases and revealed abnormal lamellar bodies in SDR9C7 and CERS3 patients.
evidence.explanation: Supports lamellar-body abnormalities in lipid-barrier ARCI genotypes.

evidence.snippet: LIPN encodes one of six acid lipases known to be involved in triglyceride metabolism in mammals . LIPN was found to be exclusively expressed in the epidermis and to be strongly induced during keratinocyte differentiation.
evidence.explanation: Places LIPN on this node: an epidermis-restricted acid lipase acting in triglyceride metabolism and induced during keratinocyte differentiation.

evidence.snippet: Deficiency of 12R-LOX and eLOX3 disrupts the epidermal barrier function and leads to an abnormal epidermal differentiation.
evidence.explanation: Places the two epidermal lipoxygenases on this node by naming the barrier and differentiation consequence of losing them.

steps/14.description: Multiple ARCI genes affect epidermal lipid metabolism, lipid transport, or acylceramide-related barrier biology. ABCA12-associated ARCI is especially severe when both alleles cause loss of function.

evidence.snippet: Caspase-14 is a protease that is mainly expressed in suprabasal epidermal layers and activated during keratinocyte cornification. Caspase-14-deficient mice display reduced epidermal barrier function and increased sensitivity to UVB radiation.
evidence.explanation: Supports the cell type, the epidermal location, the peptidase activity and the barrier consequence asserted by this node.

steps/15.description: A third branch of the ARCI cornification lesion, distinct from transglutaminase cross-linking and from epidermal lipid handling. Caspase-14 is expressed in the suprabasal epidermis and activated during keratinocyte cornification, where it performs the terminal proteolytic step that breaks filaggrin down into the free amino acids and derivatives that make up the natural moisturizing factors of the stratum corneum. Where this step fails, filaggrin fragments accumulate and natural moisturizing factors are depleted. CASP14 is the ARCI gene assigned to this branch.

evidence.explanation: The patient missense allele abolishes catalytic activity in a recombinant assay.

steps/2.description: MYSM1 deubiquitinates histone H2A lysine 119 and regulates selected gene loci. A catalytic D660N mouse retains MYSM1 protein yet reproduces many knockout phenotypes, establishing a requirement for catalytic function in hematopoiesis. This does not establish H2AK119 as the substrate for every MYSM1-dependent pathway: ribosomal-protein promoters show no significant H2AK119ub increase after knockdown, and the DNA-damage-signaling substrate remains unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Loss of p53 in mice fully rescues Mysm1-/- anemia phenotype but not RP gene expression, indicating that RP gene dysregulation is a direct outcome of Mysm1 deficiency and an upstream mediator of Mysm1-/- phenotypes through p53 activation.
evidence.explanation: Places the ribosomal-protein defect upstream of, and independent from, p53.

evidence.snippet: We characterize a patient with a homozygous nonsense MYSM1 gene variant, and we demonstrate reduced protein synthesis and increased p53 levels in patient hematopoietic cells.
evidence.explanation: Human confirmation of reduced protein synthesis and raised p53 in patient blood cells.

evidence.snippet: No significant increase in H2AK119ub levels was seen in the Mysm1-knockdown Ba/F3 cells
evidence.explanation: The measured promoter effect does not support routing this branch through H2AK119ub accumulation.

steps/3.description: MYSM1 binds promoters of ribosomal-protein and translation-factor genes and maintains their expression in mouse hematopoietic cells. Knockdown reduces H3K27ac at tested promoters without a significant increase in H2AK119ub. The expression defect persists after p53 or PUMA deletion, supporting its position upstream of the stress response.

evidence.snippet: We observed a significant reduction of OPP incorporation in Mysm1–/– HSCs, indicating reduced protein synthesis rates
evidence.explanation: In vivo mouse OPP incorporation.

evidence.snippet: This demonstrated reduction in protein synthesis rate in many leukocyte populations
evidence.explanation: Direct measurement in blood from the p.Ser290* patient.

steps/4.description: Protein synthesis is reduced in Mysm1-deficient mouse HSCs, CRISPR-edited healthy-donor human HSCs and circulating hematopoietic cells from one affected child. The human clinical assays do not specifically establish reduced translation in patient-derived HSCs.

evidence.snippet: the levels of key proteins including GPX4, SLC7A11, and FTH1 were all significantly reduced in HSPCs
evidence.explanation: These proteins were assessed in CRISPR-edited donor HSCs; reduced translation and iron/antioxidant defenses link MYSM1 loss to ferroptosis.

steps/5.description: In MYSM1-edited healthy-donor human HSCs, GPX4, SLC7A11 and FTH1 proteins decrease despite compensatory increases in their transcripts. Reduced GPX4 activity, increased labile ferrous iron and lipid peroxidation accompany the defect. This is an engineered-cell mechanism, not a patient biomarker profile.

evidence.snippet: forced Gfi1 expression in the Mysm1−/− cells at least partially restores the function of Mysm1−/− HSC
evidence.explanation: Mouse transplantation and ectopic-expression rescue support a contributing mechanism.

steps/6.description: In one mouse model, MYSM1 occupies Gfi1 regulatory elements and facilitates GATA2/RUNX1 recruitment. Reduced Gfi1 expression contributes to loss of quiescence and impaired reconstitution; ectopic Gfi1 provides partial rescue. Expression findings differ by model and maturation stage, so GFI1 is not a universal explanation for all MYSM1 phenotypes.

evidence.snippet: Mysm1 epigenetically regulated Id4 transcription by regulating histone modification at the promoter region
evidence.explanation: Mouse neural-stem-cell chromatin and expression assays.

steps/7.description: Mouse neural-stem-cell MYSM1 loss reduces Id4 expression. MYSM1 occupancy and histone changes at the Id4 promoter, followed by partial rescue with ectopic Id4, support a context-specific regulatory mechanism.

evidence.snippet: These results establish p53 activation as the driving mechanism for hematopoietic abnormalities in Mysm1 deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Double-knockout rescue identifies p53 as the driver of the haematopoietic phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, Mysm1(tm1a/tm1a) HSCs were functionally impaired, and this was associated with elevated levels of reactive oxygen species, γH2AX DNA damage marker, and p53 protein in the hematopoietic progenitors.
evidence.explanation: Elevated p53, reactive oxygen species and DNA-damage marker in Mysm1-deficient progenitors.

steps/8.description: Mysm1-deficient mouse hematopoietic cells activate p53 stress programs. p53 deletion rescues major hematopoietic defects, while PUMA deletion rescues multipotent-progenitor survival but leaves lymphopenia and part of the HSC dysfunction. MYSM1 also restrains transcription at selected p53-target promoters. Increased p53 protein was measured in blood cells from one affected child; the genetic rescue experiments are mouse studies. Thymocyte p19ARF induction is not a universal HSPC mechanism.

evidence.snippet: HSC maintenance can be fully rescued by blocking ferroptosis, despite no alteration in protein synthesis rates.
evidence.explanation: Ferroptosis is the proximate cause of HSC loss in this human model.

evidence.snippet: this selective vulnerability to ferroptosis not only underlies HSC loss in MYSM1 deficiency but also characterizes a broader liability of human HSCs
evidence.explanation: Ties the ferroptosis vulnerability to HSC loss in MYSM1 deficiency specifically.

steps/9.description: CRISPR disruption of MYSM1 in healthy-donor human HSCs induces iron-dependent lipid peroxidation and ferroptotic death. Ferroptosis inhibitors rescue HSC maintenance without restoring translation. Edited cord-blood HSC engraftment in NBSGW mice was also rescued by liproxstatin-1 cell pretreatment plus systemic administration. Neither experiment demonstrates clinical efficacy in affected patients.

evidence.snippet: MYSM1 deficiency results in a block in early B cell commitment and a defect of B cell progenitors in expression of EBF1 and other B lymphoid genes.
evidence.explanation: The early B-cell block and its EBF1 basis in Mysm1-deficient mice.

evidence.snippet: MYSM1 derepresses EBF1 transcription in B cell progenitors by orchestrating histone modifications and transcription factor recruitment to the EBF1 locus.
evidence.explanation: Molecular mechanism at the EBF1 locus.

steps/10.description: In mice MYSM1 is required cell-intrinsically at the earliest stage of B-cell commitment, where it de-represses EBF1 by remodelling histone marks and recruiting transcription factors to the EBF1 locus; Mysm1-deficient mice have a block in early B-cell development. The human counterpart is the near-absence of B cells that is the most consistent immunological finding in patients.

evidence.snippet: We demonstrated that MYSM1 is required for NK cell maturation but not for NK lineage specification and commitment.
evidence.explanation: Stage of the NK block in Mysm1-deficient mice.

evidence.snippet: Mechanistic studies revealed that the expression of transcription factor, inhibitor of DNA-binding protein (ID2), a critical factor for NK cell development, is impaired in Mysm1(-/-) NK cells.
evidence.explanation: ID2 as the MYSM1-dependent NK transcription factor.

steps/11.description: Mysm1-deficient mice have severely impaired NK-cell development: lineage commitment is intact but maturation fails, because MYSM1 is needed to recruit NFIL3 to, and maintain active chromatin at, the ID2 locus. Low NK counts in patients are the human counterpart; the ID2 mechanism has not been examined in patient cells.

evidence.snippet: MYSM1 regulates termination of DNA damage responses but does not function in DNA break generation and repair.
evidence.explanation: Places the defect in DDR termination, not repair.

evidence.snippet: Loss of MYSM1 resulted in persistent DNA damage foci and prolonged DDR signaling.
evidence.explanation: Persistent damage signalling after MYSM1 suppression.

evidence.snippet: MYSM1-deficient cells are characterized by increased sensitivity to genotoxic stress associated with sustained induction of phosphorylated p38 protein, increased reactive oxygen species production, and decreased survival following UV light-induced DNA damage.
evidence.explanation: Genotoxic hypersensitivity of patient-derived cells.

evidence.snippet: Suppression of MYSM1 in pre-B cells did not alter generation or repair of Ig DSBs. Rather, loss of MYSM1 resulted in persistent DNA damage foci and prolonged DDR signaling.
evidence.explanation: The conclusion applies to the tested ABL-transformed pre-B and U2OS systems, not all tissues.

steps/12.description: MYSM1 knockdown prolongs signaling after DNA breaks in murine ABL-transformed pre-B and human U2OS cells. Break generation and repair were preserved in the tested assays, so persistent foci are not equivalent to unrepaired breaks. The screened infant had constitutive gamma-H2AX in a B-cell subset. Separately, primary fibroblasts and EBV-transformed cells from the 2017 siblings showed prolonged UV/genotoxic stress responses. These contexts do not justify a universal statement about DNA repair or a categorical prohibition of transplant-conditioning agents.

evidence.snippet: Genetic analysis indicated that this improvement originated from a spontaneous genetic reversion of the MYSM1 mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell.
evidence.explanation: The reversion event in the patient's HSC compartment.

evidence.snippet: The patient's blood cell counts that normalized a few months after SGR remained remarkably stable over an additional period of 12 years
evidence.explanation: Durability of the rescue.

evidence.snippet: This indicates that one or a few SGR‐positive (SGR+) HSCs suffice to reconstitute and maintain a normal immuno‐haematopoietic system in a context of MYSM1 deficiency.
evidence.explanation: One or a few corrected HSCs are sufficient for full reconstitution.

steps/13.description: In one p.His656Arg patient, reversion of one mutant allele was followed by sustained hematologic and immune recovery over twelve years. The data support correction in one or a few early stem cells; an HSC versus hemangioblast origin and the precise number of founding corrected cells remain unresolved. Mutant T cells persist, especially in the double-negative gamma-delta subset. Nonhematologic abnormalities were unaffected. No CHIP-panel variant was found at follow-up, which does not establish zero future malignant risk.

evidence.snippet: Increased levels of apoptosis in Mysm1−/− MPP4 cells were fully rescued upon deletion of either p53 or Bbc3/PUMA
evidence.explanation: Mouse double-knockout comparison identifies the MPP4 death mechanism.

steps/14.description: In Mysm1-deficient mice, PUMA-dependent apoptosis depletes lymphoid-primed MPP4 cells. Puma deletion restores their viability but does not restore downstream B- and T-cell development. This must be distinguished from ferroptosis in engineered human HSCs and from the quiescence defect of mouse HSCs.

evidence.snippet: Mysm1−/− HSC loss of quiescence is rescued in Mysm1−/−p53−/− HSCs
evidence.explanation: Ki67-based analysis; PUMA deletion gives incomplete rescue.

steps/15.description: Loss of HSC quiescence and impaired long-term reconstitution occur in several Mysm1-deficient mouse models. Quiescence is only partially rescued by Puma deletion, while p53 deletion restores it. Age, genetic background and assay affect the measured cycling phenotype; hyperproliferation is not uniform across every published model.

evidence.snippet: Mysm1 deletion drives HSCs from quiescence into rapid cycling and increases their apoptotic rate, resulting in an exhaustion of the stem cell pool
evidence.explanation: HSC exhaustion in Mysm1-deficient mice.

evidence.snippet: Here we characterized an H2A-DUB targeted mouse line Mysm1(tm1a/tm1a) and demonstrated defects in BM hematopoiesis, resulting in lymphopenia, anemia, and thrombocytosis.
evidence.explanation: Marrow haematopoietic failure in the first Mysm1 mouse line.

steps/16.description: MYSM1 loss impairs hematopoietic reconstitution and maintenance in mouse transplantation assays and engineered human HSC xenografts. The number of phenotypically defined HSCs is variable across models and need not decrease; severe progenitor depletion and loss of functional capacity are more consistent. Clinical marrow hypocellularity and cytopenias are compatible with these mechanisms, but the relative contributions in patients are unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Mysm1-deficient NSCs skewed toward neurogenesis instead of astrogliogenesis
evidence.explanation: Conditional mouse and culture experiments support altered fate balance; the abstract’s generalized apoptosis claim requires the qualifications in the results.

evidence.snippet: There was no difference in the expression of apoptosis markers in NSCs before and after knockout of Mysm1 in vivo
evidence.explanation: The full text qualifies the broader wording in the abstract.

steps/17.description: Nestin-Cre Mysm1 conditional mice and cultured mouse neural stem cells show increased activation and neuronal differentiation with reduced astroglial differentiation. The stem-cell pool is depleted in the dentate-gyrus niche. Baseline apoptosis was not increased in vivo or unstimulated culture; increased apoptosis occurred after experimental challenge. The mechanism has not been demonstrated in patient neural tissue.

evidence.snippet: Increased rates of apoptosis were also detected in other tissues affected by Mysm1 deficiency, including the developing brain and the skin.
evidence.explanation: Extra-haematopoietic apoptosis in Mysm1-deficient mice.

evidence.snippet: defective B-cell development, growth retardation, neurological defects, skin atrophy, and tail malformation were almost completely restored as well
evidence.explanation: Developmental defects rescued in p53/Mysm1 double-deficient mice.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal alterations and osteopenia of Mysm1-deficient mice were phenotypically completely rescued by simultaneous ablation of p53 in p53-/-Mysm1-/- double-deficient mice
evidence.explanation: The skeletal phenotype is p53-dependent in mice.

steps/18.description: Global Mysm1-deficient mice show increased apoptosis in developing brain and skin, and p53 deletion ameliorates growth, neurologic and skin phenotypes. The contribution to human developmental manifestations is inferred. Skeletal osteopenia also improves after p53 deletion, but reduced osteoblast Runx2 expression persists and cannot be equated with correction of the primary osteoblast defect. A neural-stem-cell conditional model shows a distinct differentiation imbalance without increased baseline apoptosis in vivo.

evidence.snippet: We report four cases of MYSM1 mutations progressing from marrow failure to MDS or AML within 9-10 years.
evidence.explanation: Direct human evidence of myeloid progression.

evidence.snippet: Genetic abnormalities, including TP53 mutation and chromosomal anomalies, suggest clonal evolution.
evidence.explanation: Acquired clonal lesions at progression.

steps/19.description: Four patients from two families developed hypocellular MDS or MDS/AML at approximately ten to twelve years in a 2025 series. Findings included chromosome 7 abnormalities, trisomy 8, 5q deletion, an incompletely characterized TP53 mutation and CALR p.Pro228Ser at 50% allele fraction. Without nonhematopoietic comparison, the CALR variant is not established as an acquired driver. The series documents progression but does not prove that HSC selection, p53 escape or any specific variant caused it, and cannot quantify lifetime risk.

evidence.snippet: Most of the patients had presented with BMF characterized by anemia in 9 cases
evidence.explanation: Anaemia is the dominant presenting feature in the literature review.

evidence.snippet: Our patients initially were transfusion dependent during infancy, then showed spontaneous improvement until age 9-10 years; they became transfusion depended, which may indicate clonal evolution as showed in our patients.
evidence.explanation: The authors describe an overall biphasic course; their detailed case chronology differs, so this is not an exact timeline for every patient.

steps/20.description: Early-onset anemia is often transfusion dependent, but severity and duration vary. Some patients improve spontaneously and later develop recurrent cytopenias or myeloid neoplasia. Published reports give differing transfusion timelines for the founding siblings, so a uniform age of recovery is not inferred.

evidence.snippet: BM cellularity at initial diagnosis | 10% | 20% | 5% | 10%
evidence.explanation: Hypocellular marrow in all four patients of the series.

evidence.explanation: Primary 2022 Israeli inherited-cytopenia cohort; MYSM1 patient findings, not other cohort diagnoses.

steps/21.description: Marrow cellularity of 5 to 20% at diagnosis in the four Saudi patients.

evidence.explanation: Pancytopenia in a child with BMFS4.

evidence.explanation: Pancytopenia at one month of age.

steps/25.description: Usually mild or intermittent in patients. Mysm1-deficient mice show the opposite, thrombocytosis (see the model-mismatch discussion).

evidence.snippet: Here we describe a patient presenting with a complete lack of B lymphocytes, T-cell lymphopenia, defective hematopoiesis, and developmental abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Complete absence of B cells.

evidence.explanation: Hypogammaglobulinaemia as part of the syndrome.

evidence.explanation: Defines MYSM1 deficiency as an immunodeficiency.

evidence.explanation: Orphanet definition.

edges/1.description: Loss of MYSM1 protein, or of its catalytic site, removes its H2A deubiquitinase activity.

edges/2.description: MYSM1 maintains ribosomal-protein gene expression through promoter regulation that is not established to require local H2AK119 deubiquitination.

edges/3.description: MYSM1 loss prolongs damage signaling in the tested cell systems; the responsible substrate is unresolved.

edges/4.description: Global Mysm1 loss induces p53-dependent developmental pathology in mouse brain and skin.

edges/5.description: Neural-stem-cell MYSM1 deficiency reduces Id4 transcription in the mouse model.

edges/6.description: MYSM1 de-represses EBF1 and other early B-lineage genes.

edges/7.description: MYSM1 keeps the ID2 locus in active chromatin during NK-cell maturation.

edges/8.description: MYSM1 loss changes histone marks and transcription-factor recruitment at Gfi1 regulatory elements.

edges/9.description: Reduced expression of ribosomal components accompanies reduced protein synthesis.

edges/10.description: Ribosomal stress is a proposed upstream trigger; the expression defect persists when p53 is deleted.

evidence.snippet: Mysm1(-/-)p53(-/-) mouse characterization showed a full rescue of Mysm1(-/-) developmental and hematopoietic defects.
evidence.explanation: Lymphopenia is among the defects rescued by p53 loss.

edges/11.description: p53 deletion restores lymphopoiesis in Mysm1-deficient mice.

evidence.snippet: Mysm1(-/-) thymi were severely hypoplastic with <10% of wild-type cell numbers as a result of a reduction of early thymocyte progenitors in context with defective hematopoietic stem cells
evidence.explanation: Thymic hypoplasia in Mysm1-deficient mice, the model counterpart of T-cell lymphopenia in some patients.

edges/12.description: In mice, loss of early thymocyte progenitors and thymocyte apoptosis leave the thymus hypoplastic; both are restored by p53 deletion.

edges/13.description: PUMA is a nonredundant mediator of MPP4 apoptosis in the studied mouse model.

edges/14.description: p53 deletion restores quiescence; PUMA deletion gives only partial rescue.

edges/15.description: Ferroptotic loss reduces maintenance and engraftment of engineered human HSCs.

edges/16.description: Loss of effective hematopoietic output can contribute to hypocellularity; marrow cellularity varies by patient and stage.

evidence.snippet: Loss of p53 in mice fully rescues Mysm1-/- anemia phenotype but not RP gene expression, indicating that RP gene dysregulation is a direct outcome of Mysm1 deficiency and an upstream mediator of Mysm1-/- phenotypes through p53 activation.
evidence.explanation: The mouse anaemia depends on the p53 arm.

edges/17.description: Erythroid output falls; in mice the anaemia is fully p53-dependent.

edges/18.description: Myeloid output falls.

edges/19.description: Multilineage output falls.

edges/20.description: Megakaryocytic output falls in patients (mice differ; see discussion).

edges/21.description: All three lineages fall together in the more severe presentations.

edges/22.description: Few B cells reach the periphery.

edges/23.description: B-cell depletion can contribute to the human antibody deficiency, but a mouse model retains or enhances serum antibody responses despite lymphopenia.

edges/24.description: The humoral defect contributes to infection susceptibility.

edges/25.description: Few mature NK cells reach the circulation.

edges/26.description: Growth retardation in the mouse model; short stature in patients.

edges/27.description: Neurological defects in the mouse model; developmental delay in patients.

edges/28.description: Apoptosis in the developing mouse brain; microcephaly in patients.

edges/29.description: Hypocellular MDS in three of the four progressing patients.

edges/30.description: MDS/AML in one of the four progressing patients.

edges/31.description: Translation impairment reduces production of iron-handling and antioxidant proteins in engineered human HSCs.

edges/32.description: Loss of lipid-peroxide defenses and altered iron handling sensitize edited HSCs to ferroptotic death.

edges/33.description: Loss of downstream progenitors contributes to disturbed hematopoietic maintenance and compensatory HSC cycling.

edges/34.description: Disrupted quiescence contributes to impaired stem-cell maintenance.

edges/35.description: Reduced Gfi1 contributes to disturbed quiescence in the studied mouse model.

edges/36.description: Reduced Id4 contributes to increased neuronal differentiation and reduced astroglial differentiation.

evidence.explanation: The conditioning caution follows from the DNA-damage-response defect measured in cells; it is an inference, not a transplant outcome.

treatments/0.description: Allogeneic HSCT has restored hematopoiesis and immune function in reported children, including matched-family and haploidentical transplants. The 2017 siblings received fludarabine, treosulfan and alemtuzumab, with two-year donor engraftment. Other cases have shorter or longer follow-up and reported acute or chronic GVHD; the 2017 girl developed post-transplant Graves disease. Conditioning and timing require individual assessment of marrow disease and toxicity. Cell-assay sensitivity and analogies with other marrow-failure syndromes do not establish a universal ban on alkylators, which were used in successful transplants. Correction of all developmental features is not demonstrated.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Replaces the defective HSC compartment with donor HSCs.

treatments/5.description: Eltrombopag was started in one transfusion-dependent adolescent with hypocellular marrow, dysplasia and a TP53 mutation while haploidentical HSCT was being considered. The report provides no response assessment, so benefit in BMFS4 is undetermined.

hypotheses/0.description: MYSM1 loss reduces ribosomal-protein gene expression and translation. Mouse genetics support a p53-mediated hematopoietic-stress pathway, while edited human HSCs identify a ferroptosis pathway with reduced antioxidant and iron-handling proteins. The relationship between these pathways in patients remains unresolved. Direct clinical support for translation/p53 involvement comes from blood-cell assays in one child; neither ferroptosis inhibition nor p53 inhibition has established clinical benefit.

evidence.snippet: We report four cases of MYSM1 mutations progressing from marrow failure to MDS or AML within 9-10 years.
evidence.explanation: The only series documenting progression.

open_questions/0.rationale: The 2025 series documents four progressions from two families, including follow-up of previously reported siblings. Overlapping case ascertainment, early transplantation and somatic rescue prevent estimation of cumulative malignancy risk or an evidence-based surveillance interval.

evidence.snippet: Here we characterized an H2A-DUB targeted mouse line Mysm1(tm1a/tm1a) and demonstrated defects in BM hematopoiesis, resulting in lymphopenia, anemia, and thrombocytosis.
evidence.explanation: Thrombocytosis in the mouse.

evidence.snippet: Here, we describe a Chinese female patient who mainly presented with leukopenia, granulocytopenia, thrombocytopenia, severe anemia, and B-cell and natural killer cell deficiency in the peripheral blood, and was diagnosed with bone marrow failure.
evidence.explanation: Thrombocytopenia in a patient.

open_questions/1.rationale: The mouse reproduces the anaemia, lymphopenia and HSC failure, but the megakaryocyte lineage moves the opposite way. Either MYSM1 has a species-specific role in megakaryopoiesis, or the mouse thrombocytosis is a compensatory response absent in humans. Until that is understood, the mouse cannot be used to predict platelet-lineage behaviour.

evidence.snippet: the serum concentrations of IgM and IgG isotypes were normal or even higher in Mysm1−/− mice
evidence.explanation: Direct mouse evidence of the discordance.

open_questions/2.rationale: The mature mouse B-cell/Pax5 study shows enhanced plasma-cell differentiation and normal or higher serum Ig despite B-cell depletion. This contrasts with hypogammaglobulinemia in affected patients and prevents a simple extrapolation from B-cell number to antibody output.

evidence.snippet: No significant increase in H2AK119ub levels was seen in the Mysm1-knockdown Ba/F3 cells
evidence.explanation: Direct negative result at the tested RP promoters.

open_questions/3.rationale: Catalytic necessity is established in a mouse model, but RP promoters do not accumulate detectable H2AK119ub after knockdown, and the DDR study did not establish its proposed H2AK15 substrate. A single histone-mark route is therefore unsupported.

evidence.snippet: A near complete rescue was observed in the bone marrow, spleen, and across all lineages
evidence.explanation: Preclinical engraftment result, not clinical response.

open_questions/4.rationale: Rescue is demonstrated in engineered healthy-donor HSCs and xenografts; clinical efficacy, delivery, long-term clonal consequences and its relationship to the p53 pathway remain unresolved.

evidence.snippet: Mysm1-deficient NSCs skewed toward neurogenesis instead of astrogliogenesis
evidence.explanation: The study includes conditional mice and neural cultures; this differentiation finding is supported by its culture assays and does not establish a patient neural mechanism.

open_questions/5.rationale: Global knockout, neural-specific knockout and meander-tail mice reveal different apoptosis, fate-balance and cerebellar findings. The latter is a preprint. Patient neural tissue and a direct human cerebellar counterpart are lacking.

evidence.snippet: All mutations disrupted the tyrosine kinase domain or resulted in nonsense-mediated mRNA decay.
evidence.explanation: Across all 11 BANDDOS-associated CSF1R variants reviewed, the molecular consequence converges on loss of tyrosine kinase function or loss of the transcript, establishing loss of function as the molecular lesion.

evidence.snippet: Total CSF1R protein expression levels were normal as compared with wild-type allele, but CSF1 ligand dependent autophosphorylation was consistent with a hypomorphic allele.
evidence.explanation: Functional assay of the p.T833M allele shows normal receptor abundance but impaired ligand-dependent autophosphorylation, directly demonstrating the signalling defect in a hypomorphic BANDDOS allele.

evidence.snippet: Compared with Csf1r-null mice, the skeletal and neural phenotypes of the affected individuals appeared milder and variable, suggesting that at least one of the mutations in each affected individual is hypomorphic.
evidence.explanation: Supports the dose-dependent model: complete nullity is not what is seen clinically, and residual CSF1R activity from a hypomorphic allele sets the severity.

steps/1.description: CSF1R encodes a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase activated by two ligands, CSF1 and IL-34. In BANDDOS both alleles carry pathogenic variants - most often splice, nonsense, or deep-intronic changes that disrupt the tyrosine kinase domain or trigger nonsense-mediated decay, less often hypomorphic missense changes that leave the protein expressed but unable to autophosphorylate on ligand binding. Because complete CSF1R nullity is lethal or far more severe than what is observed clinically, at least one allele in each reported individual is thought to retain partial function, and the residual level of CSF1R signalling grades disease severity across the CSF1R-related disorder continuum.

evidence.snippet: Post-mortem examination of an individual with a homozygous splice mutation (c.1754-1G>C) demonstrated several structural brain anomalies, including agenesis of corpus callosum. Immunostaining demonstrated almost complete absence of microglia within this brain, suggesting that it developed in the absence of microglia.
evidence.explanation: Direct human neuropathological demonstration that a biallelic CSF1R brain is essentially devoid of microglia, and that development proceeded in their absence.

evidence.snippet: A single brain autopsy evidenced multiple brain anomalies, absence of corpus callosum, absence of microglia, severe white matter atrophy with axonal spheroids, gliosis, and numerous dystrophic calcifications.
evidence.explanation: Independent review confirms absence of microglia as the defining histological finding alongside the structural and degenerative changes.

evidence.snippet: We analyzed a zebrafish model (csf1rDM) lacking Csf1r function and found that their brains also lacked microglia and had reduced levels of CUX1, a neuronal transcription factor.
evidence.explanation: A vertebrate model lacking Csf1r function reproduces the microglial deficiency, supporting conservation of the cellular mechanism.

steps/2.description: Loss of CSF1R signalling prevents the establishment and expansion of the microglial population, so the fetal and postnatal brain develops with few or no microglia. Post-mortem examination of a homozygous splice-variant case showed almost complete absence of microglia, with only rare abnormal perivascular cells remaining. This is a primary microgliopathy: the initiating cellular lesion is loss of the brain's resident macrophage, not a primary defect of neurons or oligodendrocytes.

evidence.snippet: Colony stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R, MIM# 164770) encodes a tyrosine-kinase receptor playing an important role in development of osteoclasts and microglia.
evidence.explanation: States the osteoclast-development role of CSF1R that makes osteoclast failure the expected consequence of biallelic loss of function.

evidence.snippet: WT BM transfer restored osteoclasts, eliminated osteopetrosis, restored bone marrow cellularity and architecture and reversed granulocytosis and B cell deficiency.
evidence.explanation: Rescue experiment in the Csf1rko rat establishes that osteoclast deficiency is the proximate cause of the osteopetrotic bone phenotype and that it is intrinsic to bone-marrow-derived cells.

steps/3.description: Osteoclasts differentiate from the CSF1R-dependent monocyte/macrophage lineage, and CSF1-CSF1R signalling is required for their generation and survival. Reduced CSF1R signalling therefore reduces osteoclastic bone resorption, so bone formed during modelling is not removed. The result is increased bone mineral density with failure of metaphyseal remodelling - the mechanistic basis of the sclerosing bone dysplasia. In the Csf1rko rat, transfer of wild-type bone marrow restores osteoclasts and eliminates the osteopetrosis, demonstrating that the bone phenotype is cell-autonomous to the marrow-derived lineage.

evidence.snippet: Brain abnormalities included white matter changes (n = 19/19), calcifications (n = 15/18), agenesis of corpus callosum (n = 12/16), ventriculomegaly (n = 13/19), Dandy-Walker complex (n = 7/19), and cortical abnormalities (n = 4/10).
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the spectrum and frequency of congenital brain abnormalities across the reviewed BANDDOS cohort.

evidence.snippet: Compared to CSF1R-ALSP, cases with BANDDOS also displayed other congenital brain anomalies, including Dandy-Walker malformation, ventriculomegaly, and cortical abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Establishes congenital brain malformation as the discriminating feature of BANDDOS relative to the adult-onset monoallelic disorder.

evidence.snippet: The observed phenotypes for these recessive variants were novel (e.g., FBN2-related myopathy and CSF1R-related brain malformation and osteopetrosis), typical (e.g., ACTG2-related visceral myopathy), or an apparently healthy state (e.g., PDE11A), consistent with the corresponding mouse knockout phenotypes.
evidence.explanation: The first report of the recessive CSF1R phenotype names brain malformation and osteopetrosis as the novel biallelic presentation.

steps/4.description: The developmental arm of BANDDOS. Some brain abnormality is present in every reported case; the individual congenital malformations vary in frequency and include agenesis or hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly and colpocephaly, Dandy-Walker complex and large cisterna magna, cortical malformations, heterotopia, abnormal hippocampal gyration, and non-decussation of pyramidal tracts. These congenital malformations are the feature that most cleanly separates BANDDOS from adult-onset CSF1R-ALSP, in which they are not seen.

evidence.snippet: Histological evaluation evidenced severe microglia deficiency with only rare spotting of abnormal microglia around the blood vessels, prominent white matter atrophy with axonal spheroids, gliosis, and numerous dystrophic calcifications predominantly in the periventricular white matter
evidence.explanation: The single published BANDDOS brain autopsy documents white matter atrophy, axonal spheroids, gliosis, and dystrophic calcification.

evidence.snippet: During neurological decline in siblings one and two, the leukoencephalopathy was progressive and had the MRI appearance of ALSP.
evidence.explanation: Documents the progressive, ALSP-like radiological evolution of the white matter disease during secondary neurological decline.

evidence.snippet: Macroscopically both disorders shared extensive white matter degeneration, most prominent in the periventricular region, corpus callosum, and pyramidal tracts
evidence.explanation: Establishes the anatomical distribution of the white matter degeneration shared with CSF1R-ALSP.

steps/5.description: The degenerative arm of BANDDOS, superimposed on the developmental lesion. White matter changes are present in 100% of reported cases. Histology shows prominent white matter atrophy with axonal spheroids, gliosis, and numerous dystrophic calcifications concentrated in periventricular white matter - the same picture as CSF1R-ALSP but more severe. On MRI the leukoencephalopathy is progressive and takes on the appearance of ALSP at the time of secondary neurological decline.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal deformities were observed in 13/17 cases and fell within the dysosteosclerosis - Pyle disease spectrum.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies the frequency of skeletal involvement and defines its radiological spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Described skeletal findings of the disease are highly variable ranging from absence of a skeletal phenotype and milder Pyle disease-like to osteopetrosis and DOS.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the variability of the skeletal phenotype, including its complete absence in some individuals.

evidence.snippet: In addition, some individuals with bi-allelic missense mutations of CSF1R have been found to present with incomplete BANDDOS where skeletal dysplasia is absent.
evidence.explanation: Documents the incomplete-BANDDOS presentation in which biallelic missense variants spare the skeleton.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal anomalies include osteosclerosis of the craniofacial bones and skull, optic canal narrowing, kyphosis, platyspondyly and abnormalities of the long bones, e.g. undermodeling, widened metaphyses, and constricted and sclerotic diaphysis
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the specific radiographic elements of the BANDDOS skeletal phenotype, including the optic canal narrowing relevant to visual loss.

steps/6.description: The skeletal component of BANDDOS spans a spectrum: at the sclerotic end, osteopetrosis and dysosteosclerosis with generalised increased bone density; at the modelling-defect end, Pyle-disease-like metaphyseal widening with Erlenmeyer flask deformity of the long bones. Skeletal involvement is present in most but not all cases, is variable even between siblings carrying the same genotype, and may be entirely absent in individuals with hypomorphic missense alleles ("incomplete BANDDOS").

evidence.snippet: Neurological symptoms included speech disturbances (n = 13/15), cognitive decline (n = 12/14), spasticity/rigidity (n = 12/15), hyperactive tendon reflex (n = 11/14), pathological reflexes (n = 8/11), seizures (n = 9/16), dysphagia (n = 9/12), developmental delay (n = 7/14), infantile hypotonia (n = 3/11), and optic nerve atrophy (n = 2/7).
evidence.explanation: Enumerates the neurological manifestations and their frequencies across the reviewed BANDDOS cohort.

evidence.snippet: Most affected individuals eventually become bedridden with spasticity, rigidity, and loss of the ability to walk.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews describes the end-stage trajectory shared across the CSF1R-related disorder spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Three patients died in infancy, two in childhood, and one case at unspecified age.
evidence.explanation: Documents the mortality observed in the reviewed BANDDOS cohort.

steps/7.description: The clinical convergence point of the developmental and degenerative arms. Most patients present perinatally or in infancy with hypotonia, developmental delay, and seizures, then follow a course of cognitive regression, speech deterioration, spasticity and rigidity with pyramidal signs, and dysphagia. A minority with hypomorphic alleles are normal or near-normal through childhood and decline in the second or third decade, an ALSP-like trajectory. In the end stage, patients become bedridden with loss of speech and voluntary movement; several reported patients died in infancy or childhood.

evidence.snippet: Neurological symptoms included speech disturbances (n = 13/15), cognitive decline (n = 12/14), spasticity/rigidity (n = 12/15), hyperactive tendon reflex (n = 11/14), pathological reflexes (n = 8/11), seizures (n = 9/16), dysphagia (n = 9/12), developmental delay (n = 7/14), infantile hypotonia (n = 3/11), and optic nerve atrophy (n = 2/7).
evidence.explanation: Reports developmental delay in 7 of 14 assessable BANDDOS patients (50%), mapping to the FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Early-onset disease is associated with hypotonia, delayed acquisition of developmental milestones, and non-neurologic manifestations (such as skeletal abnormalities); both early- and late-onset disease have similar neurodegenerative involvement.
evidence.explanation: GeneReviews identifies delayed milestones as characteristic of the early-onset (biallelic) form of CSF1R-related disorder.

steps/8.description: Delayed acquisition of developmental milestones is a common early feature, reported in 7 of 14 assessable cases.

evidence.snippet: Progressive cognitive dysfunction was present in 86% of BANDDOS cases
evidence.explanation: Directly quantifies progressive cognitive decline at 86% of cases, mapping to the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/9.description: Progressive loss of previously acquired cognitive ability, present in 12 of 14 assessable cases (86%) and typically the dominant clinical problem.

evidence.snippet: The female child experienced acute encephalopathy at the age of 2 years, followed by spasticity and loss of all achieved milestones over 6 months.
evidence.explanation: Documents rapid regression with loss of all achieved milestones after an acute encephalopathic presentation in a biallelic CSF1R child.

steps/10.description: Loss of previously achieved milestones following an initial period of normal or near-normal development is characteristic; in one reported sibling pair all achieved milestones were lost within 6-8 months of an acute encephalopathic presentation.

evidence.snippet: Speech disturbances were the most common neurological symptom in BANDDOS and were present in 87% of cases, with dysarthria reported in more than half of cases.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies speech disturbance as a whole at 87%, mapping to the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: As all cases with BANDDOS with speech disturbances had accompanying cognitive decline or developmental delay, the multifaceted nature of speech dysfunction, as seen in CSF1R-ALSP, is most likely.
evidence.explanation: Supports the multifactorial (language plus motor speech) characterisation rather than attributing the deficit to dysarthria alone.

steps/11.description: Speech disturbance is the single most common neurological symptom in BANDDOS, reported in 87% of cases. As in CSF1R-ALSP the deficit is likely multifactorial, combining language disturbance with motor speech impairment, since every BANDDOS case with speech disturbance also had cognitive decline or developmental delay.

evidence.snippet: with dysarthria reported in more than half of cases
evidence.explanation: Dysarthria specifically is reported in more than half of cases, which maps to the FREQUENT band (30-79%) - not to the 87% VERY_FREQUENT figure, which is for speech disturbance as a whole.

steps/12.description: Motor speech impairment specifically, reported in more than half of BANDDOS cases - a subset of the broader 87% with speech disturbance.

evidence.snippet: Pyramidal signs (spasticity, hyperactive tendon reflexes, and pathological reflexes) were present in up to 80% of BANDDOS cases
evidence.explanation: Quantifies pyramidal signs at up to 80% of cases, mapping to the VERY_FREQUENT band.

steps/13.description: Pyramidal and extrapyramidal motor signs, present in 12 of 15 assessable cases; together with hyperreflexia and pathological reflexes, pyramidal signs occur in up to 80% of patients.

evidence.snippet: hyperactive tendon reflex (n = 11/14)
evidence.explanation: Reports hyperactive tendon reflexes in 11 of 14 assessable cases (79%), mapping to the FREQUENT band.

steps/14.description: Hyperactive tendon reflexes were documented in 11 of 14 assessable cases.

evidence.snippet: Seizures were noted in 56% of cases in BANDDOS, compared to up to 32% of CSF1R-ALSP
evidence.explanation: Quantifies seizure frequency at 56%, mapping to the FREQUENT band, and contrasts it with the adult-onset form.

evidence.snippet: Patients presented with developmental delay, therapy-resistant epilepsy, dysmorphic features, and skeletal abnormalities.
evidence.explanation: Documents therapy-resistant epilepsy as a presenting feature in a three-sibling BANDDOS family.

steps/15.description: Seizures occur in about 56% of BANDDOS patients, a higher proportion than in adult-onset CSF1R-ALSP, and may be therapy-resistant.

evidence.snippet: Dysphagia was common and reported in 75% of cases of BANDDOS
evidence.explanation: Quantifies dysphagia at 75% of cases, mapping to the FREQUENT band.

steps/16.description: Swallowing difficulty is common (75% of BANDDOS cases, versus 18% in CSF1R-ALSP) and contributes to aspiration risk.

evidence.snippet: In addition, a minority of BANDDOS cases presented infantile hypotonia (27%) and atrophy of the optic nerve (29%), which were not reported in CSF1R-ALSP.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies infantile hypotonia at 27%, mapping to the OCCASIONAL band, and marks it as a BANDDOS-specific feature.

steps/17.description: Generalised hypotonia in infancy was reported in about 27% of cases and is not a feature of adult-onset CSF1R-ALSP.

evidence.snippet: callosal abnormalities (agenesis in 75% of BANDDOS vs. atrophy in 29% with CSF1R-ALSP cases)
evidence.explanation: Quantifies callosal agenesis at 75%, mapping to the FREQUENT band, and distinguishes it from the atrophy pattern of CSF1R-ALSP.

steps/18.description: Callosal agenesis is a congenital, developmental feature of BANDDOS, present in 12 of 16 assessable cases (75%), and contrasts with the callosal atrophy seen in adult-onset CSF1R-ALSP. It is the single most useful radiological discriminator between the two disorders.

evidence.snippet: Brain abnormalities included white matter changes (n = 19/19), calcifications (n = 15/18), agenesis of corpus callosum (n = 12/16), ventriculomegaly (n = 13/19), Dandy-Walker complex (n = 7/19), and cortical abnormalities (n = 4/10).
evidence.explanation: Reports ventriculomegaly in 13 of 19 BANDDOS patients (68%), mapping to the FREQUENT band.

steps/19.description: Enlargement of the lateral ventricles, often with colpocephaly, reported in 13 of 19 cases.

evidence.snippet: Brain abnormalities included white matter changes (n = 19/19), calcifications (n = 15/18), agenesis of corpus callosum (n = 12/16), ventriculomegaly (n = 13/19), Dandy-Walker complex (n = 7/19), and cortical abnormalities (n = 4/10).
evidence.explanation: Reports Dandy-Walker complex in 7 of 19 BANDDOS patients (37%), mapping to the FREQUENT band.

steps/20.description: Posterior fossa malformation ranging from a large cisterna magna to full Dandy-Walker malformation, reported in 7 of 19 cases.

evidence.snippet: Brain abnormalities included white matter changes (n = 19/19), calcifications (n = 15/18), agenesis of corpus callosum (n = 12/16), ventriculomegaly (n = 13/19), Dandy-Walker complex (n = 7/19), and cortical abnormalities (n = 4/10).
evidence.explanation: Reports cortical abnormalities in 4 of 10 assessable cases (40%), mapping to the FREQUENT band.

steps/21.description: Cortical abnormalities including heterotopia and abnormal gyration were reported in 4 of 10 assessable cases.

evidence.snippet: numerous periventricular and brainstem calcifications, and heterotopia, abnormal gyration of hippocampi, and non-decussation of small pyramidal tracts
evidence.explanation: Autopsy documentation of heterotopia. Only one BANDDOS autopsy has been published, so no frequency band is asserted.

steps/22.description: Neuronal heterotopia was documented at autopsy alongside abnormal hippocampal gyration and non-decussation of the pyramidal tracts, part of the cortical-malformation component of the developmental arm.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal abnormalities were observed in 76% of cases of BANDDOS.
evidence.explanation: Quantifies skeletal involvement at 76% of BANDDOS cases. No frequency band is asserted for osteopetrosis specifically: the 76% figure covers the whole dysosteosclerosis-Pyle spectrum, of which frank osteosclerosis is only one pole, and the sclerotic subset is not separately counted.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal survey revealed osteosclerosis, most severe in sibling three.
evidence.explanation: Independent family report documenting osteosclerosis on skeletal survey, with intrafamilial variability in severity.

steps/23.description: Generalised increased bone density due to deficient osteoclastic resorption; the sclerotic end of the BANDDOS skeletal spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Described skeletal findings of the disease are highly variable ranging from absence of a skeletal phenotype and milder Pyle disease-like to osteopetrosis and DOS.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the Pyle-disease-like metaphyseal modelling defect as one end of the BANDDOS skeletal spectrum. No cohort-level frequency is reported for this specific radiographic sign, so no frequency band is asserted.

evidence.snippet: Skeletal anomalies include osteosclerosis of the craniofacial bones and skull, optic canal narrowing, kyphosis, platyspondyly and abnormalities of the long bones, e.g. undermodeling, widened metaphyses, and constricted and sclerotic diaphysis
evidence.explanation: Names widened metaphyses and long-bone undermodelling among the BANDDOS skeletal anomalies, directly supporting the metaphyseal widening term.

steps/24.description: The modelling-defect (Pyle-disease-like) end of the skeletal spectrum, with undertubulation and flaring of the long bone metaphyses.

evidence.snippet: calcifications (in 83% of BANDDOS vs. 75% with CSF1R-ALSP cases)
evidence.explanation: Quantifies intracranial calcification at 83% of BANDDOS cases, mapping to the VERY_FREQUENT band.

evidence.snippet: Brain imaging in both children revealed multiple well-defined areas of calcification in the parietal and frontal regions and the occipital horns of both lateral ventricles.
evidence.explanation: Describes the anatomical distribution of the calcifications in a biallelic CSF1R sibling pair.

steps/25.description: Dystrophic calcifications, predominantly periventricular and in the brainstem, are present in 15 of 18 assessable cases and are already present at birth, sharing the stepping-stone appearance seen in CSF1R-ALSP.

evidence.snippet: Brain abnormalities were present in all cases (n = 19) on neuroimaging, including white matter changes (n = 19/19)
evidence.explanation: Establishes white matter abnormality as present in 100% (19/19) of reported BANDDOS cases, the one obligate feature of the disorder.

steps/26.description: Cerebral white matter abnormality is the one universal finding in BANDDOS, present in every reported case on neuroimaging, and progresses over time to an ALSP-like appearance.

evidence.snippet: Both microglia of the central nervous system and osteoclasts stem from the monocyte phagocytic system, and their differentiation process depends on CSF1R.
evidence.explanation: States the dependence of microglial differentiation on CSF1R that makes this causal edge direct.

edges/1.description: Microglia depend on CSF1R for their proliferation, differentiation, and survival, so loss of receptor signalling depletes the brain of its resident macrophage population.

evidence.snippet: Colony stimulating factor 1 receptor (CSF1R) plays key roles in regulating development and function of the monocyte/macrophage lineage, including microglia and osteoclasts.
evidence.explanation: Establishes osteoclasts as a CSF1R-dependent lineage, grounding the causal edge from receptor loss of function to osteoclast failure.

edges/2.description: Osteoclasts arise from the same CSF1R-dependent monocyte/macrophage lineage, so the same receptor lesion compromises osteoclastogenesis.

evidence.snippet: Since a large fraction of CUX1+ neurons project callosal axons, we speculate that microglia deficiency may contribute to agenesis of the corpus callosum via reduction in CUX1+ neurons.
evidence.explanation: The authors explicitly frame the microglia-to-callosal-agenesis link as a speculative mechanism via CUX1+ neuron loss, so the edge is supported only partially and its intermediates remain unproven.

evidence.snippet: Our results suggest that CSF1R is required for human brain development
evidence.explanation: Supports the general claim that CSF1R (and hence microglia) is required for normal human brain development. The quote is deliberately trimmed to the human clause; the rest of the sentence concerns the zebrafish model and is cited separately as MODEL_ORGANISM evidence.

edges/3.description: In the absence of microglia the developing brain fails to form normal commissural, ventricular, and posterior-fossa structures. One proposed intermediate is a reduction in CUX1-positive upper-layer neurons, many of which project callosal axons.

evidence.snippet: Likewise, histological evaluation evidenced a deficiency of microglia in the brain parenchyma, atrophic white matter with axonal spheroids, gliosis, and dystrophic calcifications in BANDDOS and CSF1R-ALSP
evidence.explanation: Directly couples parenchymal microglial deficiency with the white matter degeneration, spheroids, gliosis, and calcification seen in both CSF1R disorders.

edges/4.description: The same microglial deficiency that disrupts development also leaves the white matter without its resident phagocyte, producing the progressive leukoencephalopathy that is neuropathologically indistinguishable from CSF1R-ALSP.

evidence.snippet: BANDDOS presents with variable dysmorphic features, skeletal dysplasia, developmental delay, and epilepsy with on neuro-imaging developmental brain anomalies, multifocal white matter abnormalities, and calcifications.
evidence.explanation: Links the developmental brain anomalies to the developmental delay and epilepsy that constitute the initial clinical disease.
