evidence.explanation: Shows that KDM6B/JMJD3 directly controls the neurodevelopmental transcriptional programme at promoters and enhancers.

evidence.snippet: In Jmjd3-deleted SVZ cells, I12b remains enriched with H3K27me3 and Dlx2-dependent neurogenesis fails.
evidence.explanation: Direct demonstration that loss of the demethylase leaves a neurogenic enhancer H3K27me3-marked and its target gene programme unexecuted.

evidence.snippet: KDM6B encodes a histone demethylase, expressed in different tissues during development, which regulates gene expression through the modulation of chromatin accessibility by RNA polymerase.
evidence.explanation: Clinical-genetics framing of the same chromatin-accessibility mechanism in the context of this disorder.

steps/4.description: KDM6B occupies promoters and neural enhancer elements of genes that specify neural identity, and its demethylase activity converts these elements from a poised or bivalent state to an active one. Loss of KDM6B leaves these regulatory elements enriched for H3K27me3 and inaccessible, so the transcriptional programme for neural commitment is not executed at the right time. The clinical literature describes the same principle as modulation of chromatin accessibility by RNA polymerase.

evidence.snippet: Starting from a comprehensive profiling of JmjC-domain genes, we report here that Jmjd3, recently identified as a H3-K27me3 specific demethylase, controls the expression of key regulators and markers of neurogenesis and is required for commitment to the neural lineage.
evidence.explanation: Establishes a requirement for KDM6B/Jmjd3 in neural lineage commitment.

evidence.snippet: However, KDM6-deficient NPCs exhibit poor proliferation and a failure to differentiate into neurons and glia.
evidence.explanation: Human stem cell evidence that loss of KDM6 demethylases blocks progenitor proliferation and neuronal/glial differentiation.

evidence.snippet: JMJD3 is upregulated in neuroblasts, and Jmjd3 deletion targeted to SVZ NSCs in both developing and adult mice impairs neuronal differentiation.
evidence.explanation: In vivo requirement for the demethylase in developmental and adult neurogenesis.

steps/5.description: KDM6B activity is required for cells to commit to the neural lineage and for neural progenitors to proliferate and differentiate into neurons and glia. Human embryonic stem cell-derived progenitors lacking KDM6 enzymes still form neural progenitors but proliferate poorly and fail to make neurons and glia; in mice, deletion of Jmjd3 in subventricular zone neural stem cells impairs neuronal differentiation in both the developing and the adult brain.

evidence.snippet: Here we show that the chromatin regulator KDM6B is required for both the establishment and maintenance of NSCs in the mouse DG.
evidence.explanation: Establishes the neural stem cell maintenance requirement that this node asserts. Preprint (bioRxiv), so the node is graded PROVISIONAL.

evidence.snippet: Conditional deletion of Kdm6b in embryonic DG precursors results in an adult hippocampus that is essentially devoid of NSCs, and hippocampal-dependent behaviors are defective.
evidence.explanation: Links stem cell pool depletion to a behavioral deficit, the connection this node's downstream edge asserts.

evidence.snippet: causes precocious neuronal differentiation, and the NSC population fails to become established in the postnatal DG.
evidence.explanation: Names the precocious-differentiation mechanism that distinguishes this node from the differentiation-block node.

evidence.snippet: Using single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), we observed that Kdm6b -deletion disrupts the transcriptomic signature of NSC maintenance.
evidence.explanation: Single-cell transcriptomic evidence that the neural stem cell maintenance programme itself is disrupted, which is what connects this node upstream to dysregulated neurodevelopmental gene expression. The space before "-deletion" reproduces the cached text, where the italicised gene symbol sits on its own line.

steps/6.description:
A second, direction-opposite consequence of KDM6B loss in the neural stem cell compartment. In the mouse hippocampal dentate gyrus, KDM6B is required to establish and maintain the neural stem cell pool: conditional deletion in embryonic dentate gyrus precursors causes precocious neuronal differentiation so that the stem cell population never becomes established, leaving the adult hippocampus essentially devoid of neural stem cells, with defective hippocampal-dependent behavior. Deletion in adult dentate gyrus neural stem cells likewise induces early differentiation and failure of pool maintenance.
This is deliberately modeled as a node distinct from "Impaired Neural Commitment and Neurogenesis": that node captures a differentiation block (progenitors fail to become neurons), whereas this one captures premature differentiation that exhausts the progenitor reserve. Both are reported for KDM6B loss in different compartments and developmental windows, and reconciling them is an open question recorded in the kdm6b_commitment_direction_paradox discussion. The node is PROVISIONAL because the supporting study is a mouse preprint.

evidence.snippet: Moreover, KDM6B mosaic knockout display abnormalities in hippocampal excitatory synaptic transmission decreasing NMDA receptor mediated synaptic transmission and plasticity.
evidence.explanation: Direct electrophysiological evidence linking KDM6B loss to reduced excitatory synaptic transmission and plasticity.

evidence.snippet: Consistent with the role of KDM6B in human cognition, we demonstrated a role for the Drosophila KDM6B ortholog in memory and behavior.
evidence.explanation: Cross-species evidence that the KDM6B orthologue is required for memory and behavior, consistent with a circuit-level function.

steps/7.description: Beyond its developmental role, KDM6B loss perturbs mature circuit function. Mosaic brain knockout of KDM6B in mice reduces NMDA receptor-mediated excitatory synaptic transmission and plasticity in the hippocampus, providing a cellular substrate for the cognitive and behavioral phenotype. This node is marked provisional because the evidence is currently from rodent and fly models rather than from human tissue.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, morpholino oligonucleotide inhibition of a zebrafish UTX homologue resulted in mis-regulation of hox genes and a striking posterior developmental defect, which was partially rescued by wild-type, but not by catalytically inactive, human UTX.
evidence.explanation: Model-organism evidence that loss of KDM6-family H3K27 demethylase activity mis-regulates hox genes and disturbs body patterning; tagged INDIRECT because it concerns the paralogue UTX in zebrafish, not KDM6B in human limb or face.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that the demethylase activity of Jmjd3, but not that of Utx, affects mouse axial patterning in concert with alterations in Hox gene expression.
evidence.explanation: The strongest patterning evidence for this node: loss of demethylase activity of the KDM6B orthologue itself mis-patterns the mouse axial skeleton via Hox de-repression failure. Tagged INDIRECT because the model is a homozygous mouse embryo rather than the human heterozygous state.

evidence.snippet: Notably, coarse facies and distal skeletal anomalies, as defined by OMIM, are rare in this expanded cohort while other features are unexpectedly common (e.g., hypotonia, psychosis, etc.).
evidence.explanation: Establishes that the dysmorphic and skeletal arm of the phenotype exists but is uncommon, justifying the low-confidence, minority-pathway framing of this node.

steps/8.description: A minority of affected individuals have coarse facial features, mild distal skeletal anomalies (broad hands, syndactyly, clinodactyly), and axial skeletal findings (scoliosis, pectus excavatum, supernumerary ribs). A plausible mechanism is loss of KDM6-dependent de-repression of HOX and other patterning loci: H3K27me3 controls Hox gene expression and body patterning, inhibition of the KDM6 paralogue UTX in zebrafish causes hox mis-regulation with a posterior developmental defect, and Jmjd3 mutant mouse embryos show reduced Hox expression with anterior homeotic transformation of the axial skeleton. This route has not been demonstrated for KDM6B in human craniofacial or limb development, and the 85-individual cohort showed these features to be uncommon, so the node is explicitly hypothetical.

evidence.snippet: Cognitive deficits are seen consistently in all individuals, but the overall phenotype is highly variable.
evidence.explanation: Defines the organism-level output of the mechanism: obligate cognitive involvement on a variable background.

steps/9.description: The convergent organism-level consequence: near-universal cognitive involvement with highly variable additional features, including global developmental delay, motor and speech delay, hypotonia, autism spectrum disorder, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder, psychosis in older individuals, occasional seizures, and, in a minority, coarse facies and mild distal skeletal anomalies.

evidence.snippet: Cognitive deficits are seen consistently in all individuals, but the overall phenotype is highly variable.
evidence.explanation: The 85-individual cohort reports cognitive deficits in every affected individual, which maps to the VERY_FREQUENT (80-100%) band.

steps/10.description: Cognitive involvement is the one consistent feature of the disorder, reported in every individual in the definitive 85-person cohort. Severity is variable and most affected individuals fall in the mild range.

evidence.snippet: a cohort of 12 unrelated patients with developmental delay, intellectual disability, dysmorphic facial features, and other clinical findings
evidence.explanation: Intellectual disability was one of the defining features of the founding case series.

evidence.snippet: There was usually some degree of intellectual disability evident in the older patients who had been evaluated although this was variable in severity.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports both the substantial-proportion claim and the variable severity described for this phenotype.

steps/11.description: Formally diagnosed intellectual disability is present in a substantial proportion of individuals and is variable in severity, though usually mild; learning difficulties without a formal ID diagnosis are common in the remainder. No frequency band is asserted because the cohort abstract does not quantify the ID subset separately from the broader cognitive-deficit statement.

evidence.snippet: We have identified a number of de novo alterations in the KDM6B gene via whole exome sequencing (WES) in a cohort of 12 unrelated patients with developmental delay, intellectual disability, dysmorphic facial features, and other clinical findings.
evidence.explanation: Developmental delay was the presenting feature of all 12 patients in the founding series.

steps/12.description: Developmental delay affecting multiple streams, typically recognised in infancy or early childhood, was present in all 12 patients of the founding series.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we report a case series of 12 patients presenting with neurodevelopmental delays in speech and motor development
evidence.explanation: Explicitly names speech delay as a defining feature of the reported cohort.

steps/13.description: Speech and language delay is one of the two developmental streams highlighted in the original description of the syndrome.

evidence.snippet: In this study, we report a case series of 12 patients presenting with neurodevelopmental delays in speech and motor development
evidence.explanation: Explicitly names motor delay as a defining feature of the reported cohort.

steps/14.description: Delayed acquisition of gross motor milestones, commonly delayed independent walking.

evidence.snippet: Notably, coarse facies and distal skeletal anomalies, as defined by OMIM, are rare in this expanded cohort while other features are unexpectedly common (e.g., hypotonia, psychosis, etc.).
evidence.explanation: Identifies hypotonia as an unexpectedly common feature of the expanded cohort. The statement is qualitative, so no FrequencyEnum band is assigned.

evidence.snippet: Neuromuscular hypotonia was also often present.
evidence.explanation: The founding series independently reports hypotonia as a frequent finding across its 12 patients.

steps/15.description: Hypotonia is described by the largest cohort as unexpectedly common relative to the original OMIM-derived description of the syndrome, and can be marked enough to prompt a neuromuscular workup. No numeric frequency is quoted in the retrievable abstract, so no frequency band is asserted here.

evidence.snippet: Notably, coarse facies and distal skeletal anomalies, as defined by OMIM, are rare in this expanded cohort while other features are unexpectedly common (e.g., hypotonia, psychosis, etc.).
evidence.explanation: The definitive cohort explicitly names psychosis as a feature of the KDM6B-related NDD phenotype, contradicting its omission from the OMIM-derived syndrome name.

steps/16.description: Psychosis is a distinctive and clinically actionable feature of this chromatinopathy, and its omission from the OMIM-derived syndrome name is one of the reasons that name is considered misleading. OMIM records psychosis in a small percentage of individuals older than 12 years, and the 85-individual cohort lists psychosis among the features that are unexpectedly common relative to the original syndrome description. Because the retrievable abstract characterises this only qualitatively, no frequency band is asserted (see docs/frequency-evidence-guidelines.md).

evidence.snippet: behavioral traits relatable to oppositional defiant, autism spectrum, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorders
evidence.explanation: Human case with a de novo pathogenic KDM6B variant showing autism spectrum behavioral traits.

evidence.snippet: Recent genetic and clinical studies report that KDM6B, a gene encoding a histone H3 lysine 27-specific demethylase, is one of the highest ASD risk genes.
evidence.explanation: Reports the standing of KDM6B among autism risk genes. Tagged OTHER rather than HUMAN_CLINICAL because this is a background statement in the introduction of a mouse study, not human clinical data generated by the cited publication; the primary human sequencing studies it refers to do not name KDM6B in their abstracts, so no quotable human-genetic source could be substituted.

evidence.snippet: Here we use an animal model to show that genetic deletion of one Kdm6b allele in mice leads to autistic-like impaired sociability and object recognition memory.
evidence.explanation: Heterozygous, dosage-matched mouse model reproduces autistic-like behavior, supporting causality of KDM6B haploinsufficiency.

steps/17.description: Autism spectrum disorder is a common behavioral feature. KDM6B is among the highest-confidence autism risk genes in large sequencing studies, and autistic-like phenotypes are reproduced by Kdm6b loss in mice.

evidence.snippet: The case was oriented as a neurodevelopmental disorder secondary to a genetic alteration and a comorbid Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD).
evidence.explanation: Human case with a KDM6B frameshift variant and formally assessed comorbid ADHD.

evidence.snippet: In addition, the mutant mice display markedly increased locomotor activity and impulsivity, two ADHD-like behavioral traits that are ameliorated by methylphenidate treatment.
evidence.explanation: Mouse haploinsufficiency model reproduces ADHD-like hyperactivity and impulsivity.

steps/18.description: ADHD-type inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity are recurrent behavioral features, documented in individual patients and reproduced in the heterozygous mouse model.

evidence.snippet: dysmorphic facial features including a prominent nasal bridge or nose, coarse features, as well as widened hands and syndactyly
evidence.explanation: Original description of the coarse facial features in KDM6B variant carriers.

evidence.snippet: Notably, coarse facies and distal skeletal anomalies, as defined by OMIM, are rare in this expanded cohort
evidence.explanation: Qualifies the feature as present but uncommon once ascertainment bias is removed. No frequency band is asserted because the abstract gives no numerator.

steps/19.description: Coarse facies gave the disorder its OMIM name and was prominent in the original 12-patient series, but is uncommon in the expanded 85-individual cohort. It is non-pathognomonic and can prompt an initial suspicion of a lysosomal storage disorder.

evidence.snippet: dysmorphic facial features including a prominent nasal bridge or nose
evidence.explanation: Directly reports the prominent nasal bridge or nose in the KDM6B cohort.

steps/20.description: A prominent nasal bridge or nose was among the recurring dysmorphic features in the founding case series. Like the other dysmorphic features of this disorder it is mild and does not amount to a recognisable facial gestalt.

evidence.snippet: as well as widened hands and syndactyly with de novo variants in the KDM6B gene
evidence.explanation: Reports widened hands as a recurrent distal skeletal feature in the original cohort.

steps/21.description: Widened hands were a recurrent distal limb finding in the founding series and contributed the "mild distal skeletal abnormalities" component of the OMIM name; like coarse facies, the finding is uncommon in the expanded cohort.

evidence.snippet: as well as widened hands and syndactyly with de novo variants in the KDM6B gene
evidence.explanation: Reports syndactyly among the distal limb findings of the original cohort.

steps/22.description: Syndactyly, most often of the toes, was reported in the founding series and in the earliest published individual with a KDM6B variant.

evidence.snippet: exhibiting facial dysmorphisms, dysgraphia, behavioral traits relatable to oppositional defiant, autism spectrum, and attention deficit hyperactivity disorders, a single seizure episode
evidence.explanation: Documents a seizure episode in a genetically confirmed patient.

evidence.snippet: There was a history of febrile seizures as well.
evidence.explanation: Documents febrile seizures in a patient of the founding series (Patient 1), one of the seizure types named in this phenotype's description.

evidence.snippet:
The pro-
band had a history of partial symptomatic epilepsy with complex par-
tial seizures with an abnormal EEG.
evidence.explanation: Documents partial epilepsy with an abnormal EEG in a second patient of the founding series (Patient 8). The hyphenated line breaks reproduce the cached PDF text verbatim.

steps/23.description: Seizures are an occasional, non-defining feature; reported events include febrile seizures, partial seizures with an abnormal EEG, and isolated seizure episodes. Routine EEG in an asymptomatic carrier is not indicated.

evidence.snippet: a neuroimaging finding of a single cerebellar heterotopic nodule, never described to date in this genetic condition
evidence.explanation: Single-patient observation, explicitly novel and therefore not generalisable, so no frequency is asserted.

steps/24.description: Neuroimaging findings in this disorder are generally nonspecific. A single cerebellar heterotopic nodule has been reported in one patient, the first such observation in this condition, suggesting a possible role for KDM6B in cerebellar development. HPO has no cerebellum-specific heterotopia term, so the general gray matter heterotopia term is used with a more specific preferred_term.

evidence.snippet: characterized by non-pathognomonic facial and body dysmorphisms, a wide range of neurodevelopmental and behavioral disorders and nonspecific neuroradiological findings
evidence.explanation: States directly that the dysmorphism is non-pathognomonic and the neuroradiology nonspecific.

steps/25.description: Facial and body dysmorphisms in this disorder are explicitly non-pathognomonic; no diagnostic facial gestalt exists, which is why the condition is essentially never recognised clinically without sequencing.

evidence.snippet: The proband had a pectus excavatum, a torticollis with a right head deviation, scoliosis, and an extra rib on each side.
evidence.explanation: Documents scoliosis, alongside other axial skeletal anomalies, in a KDM6B variant carrier.

steps/26.description: Spinal curvature is part of the skeletal spectrum, reported together with other axial anomalies such as pectus excavatum and supernumerary ribs.

evidence.snippet: widened and thickened hands and fingers, joint hypermobility, clinodactyly of the fifth fingers, and toe syndactyly
evidence.explanation: Names fifth-finger clinodactyly among the musculoskeletal features present in a subset of the cohort.

steps/27.description: Fifth-finger clinodactyly is part of the mild distal limb spectrum that gave the disorder its OMIM name, present in some but not all cases.

evidence.snippet: Dysmorphic facial features that were reported included coarse features, a prominent forehead, broad mouth, large and prominent ears, a round face, prognathism, and epicanthal folds.
evidence.explanation: Lists large and prominent ears in the summary of dysmorphic facial features across the cohort.

steps/28.description: Large and prominent ears are among the recurrent, individually non-diagnostic dysmorphic features.

evidence.snippet: Dysmorphic facial features that were reported included coarse features, a prominent forehead, broad mouth, large and prominent ears, a round face, prognathism, and epicanthal folds.
evidence.explanation: Lists a prominent forehead in the summary of dysmorphic facial features across the cohort.

steps/29.description: A prominent forehead is among the recurrent, individually non-diagnostic dysmorphic features.

evidence.snippet: Dysmorphic facial features that were reported included coarse features, a prominent forehead, broad mouth, large and prominent ears, a round face, prognathism, and epicanthal folds.
evidence.explanation: Lists prognathism in the summary of dysmorphic facial features across the cohort.

steps/30.description: Prognathism is among the recurrent, individually non-diagnostic dysmorphic features.

edges/1.description: Reduced KDM6B enzyme dosage or catalytic competence directly lowers the rate at which H3K27me2/me3 is erased from target loci.

edges/2.description: Persistent H3K27me3 at developmental loci means PRC2-deposited repression is no longer counterbalanced by demethylation.

edges/3.description: Sustained Polycomb repression at lineage-specifying loci prevents their timely activation.

edges/4.description: Polycomb and H3K27me3 control of HOX and other patterning loci provides a plausible but not directly demonstrated route from KDM6B loss to the dysmorphic and skeletal features seen in a minority of patients.

edges/5.description: Failure to activate neurogenic regulators blocks progression of progenitors into neurons and glia.

edges/6.description: In the hippocampal dentate gyrus the same loss of KDM6B-dependent regulation disrupts the transcriptomic signature of neural stem cell maintenance, so progenitors differentiate early instead of being held in reserve.

edges/7.description: Neurons produced from a KDM6B-deficient progenitor pool show downstream deficits in excitatory synaptic transmission and plasticity.

edges/8.description: Defective neurogenesis and neuronal differentiation underlie the cognitive and developmental features of the disorder.

edges/9.description: Delay across multiple developmental streams is the early-childhood expression of defective neurogenesis and neuronal differentiation.

edges/10.description: Gross motor delay, commonly delayed independent walking, is attributed to the same defective neural development.

evidence.snippet: These findings expand the phenotypic spectrum of this syndrome, highlighting the potential role for KDM6B in cerebellar development and providing valuable insights for genetic counseling.
evidence.explanation: The reporting authors' own developmental interpretation of the heterotopic nodule; INDIRECT because it is a single-case plausibility argument, not a demonstrated mechanism.

edges/11.description: A single reported cerebellar heterotopic nodule plausibly reflects disturbance of KDM6B-dependent neural differentiation and migration during cerebellar development, as the case report itself proposes. The route is undemonstrated and rests on one patient, so this edge is deliberately weak.

edges/12.description: Loss of the hippocampal neural stem cell reserve is accompanied by defective hippocampal-dependent behavior in the mouse, offering a substrate for the cognitive phenotype that is separate from the synaptic one.

edges/13.description: Impaired excitatory synaptic transmission and plasticity plausibly contribute to the cognitive deficits and behavioral features.

edges/14.description: Reduced NMDA receptor-mediated excitatory transmission and plasticity is the most proximal documented substrate for the obligate cognitive involvement; the supporting electrophysiology is from rodent and fly models, so the human route is inferred.

edges/15.description: Formally diagnosed intellectual disability is the severer end of the same cognitive impairment; learning difficulties without a formal diagnosis occupy the milder end.

edges/16.description: Contributes the dysmorphic and distal skeletal component of the composite clinical phenotype.

edges/17.description: Hypothesised route to the coarse facies seen in a minority of patients; no human KDM6B craniofacial study has tested it.

edges/18.description: Hypothesised route to the recurring mild nasal dysmorphism of the founding series.

edges/19.description: Hypothesised route to this recurrent, individually non-diagnostic facial feature.

edges/20.description: Hypothesised route to the large and prominent ears reported across the founding cohort.

edges/21.description: Hypothesised route to the prognathism reported in a subset of the founding cohort.

edges/22.description: The same hypothesised patterning disturbance, expressed as mild, non-pathognomonic dysmorphism rather than a diagnostic gestalt.

edges/23.description: Hypothesised route to the widened hands that contributed the "mild distal skeletal abnormalities" component of the OMIM name.

edges/24.description: Hypothesised route to the digit-separation anomaly, a classic limb-patterning phenotype.

edges/25.description: Hypothesised route to the fifth-finger clinodactyly of the mild distal limb spectrum.

evidence.snippet: Here, we report that Jmjd3, but not Utx, is involved in axial skeletal formation in mice.
evidence.explanation: Direct mouse evidence that the KDM6B orthologue patterns the axial skeleton; INDIRECT for this edge because the mouse data are homozygous embryonic homeotic transformations, not heterozygous human scoliosis.

edges/26.description: Axial skeletal anomalies (scoliosis, pectus excavatum, supernumerary ribs) are the arm of the skeletal spectrum with the most direct model-organism support, since Jmjd3 demethylase activity is required for Hox-dependent axial skeletal patterning in mouse embryos; the human route remains undemonstrated.

edges/27.description: Speech and language delay is one of the two developmental streams affected in essentially all reported children.

edges/28.description: Hypotonia is an unexpectedly common component of the composite neurodevelopmental presentation; its specific neuromuscular substrate has not been delineated.

edges/29.description: Autistic features are a recurrent behavioral component of the composite phenotype, and dosage-matched Kdm6b heterozygous mice reproduce autistic-like sociability and memory deficits.

edges/30.description: ADHD-type inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity are recurrent behavioral components, reproduced as methylphenidate-responsive hyperactivity and impulsivity in the heterozygous mouse.

edges/31.description: Psychosis in older individuals is an unexpectedly common manifestation of the disorder; the route from the chromatin lesion to psychosis is not delineated (see the kdm6b_psychosis_frequency discussion).

edges/32.description: Seizures are an occasional manifestation of the underlying brain disorder (febrile, partial, and isolated events are reported); no specific epileptogenic mechanism has been delineated.

evidence.snippet: The KDM6B protein consists of the JmjC catalytic domain and C-terminal helix and zinc motifs which are important in cofactor binding and protein stability
evidence.explanation: Defines the functional domain architecture in which the disease-associated missense and in-frame variants cluster.

evidence.snippet: indicating that haploinsufficiency of the KDM6B gene is not tolerated
evidence.explanation: Population-constraint evidence (gnomAD observed/expected loss-of-function score) that KDM6B is dosage sensitive, the premise of the haploinsufficiency mechanism. Tagged COMPUTATIONAL because the claim comes from a population-database constraint metric rather than a patient observation.

evidence.snippet: Using 3D protein structure analysis and an innovative dual Drosophila gain-of-function assay, we demonstrated a disruptive effect of 11 missense/in-frame indels located in or near the enzymatic JmJC or Zn-containing domain of KDM6B.
evidence.explanation: Functional assay evidence that disease-associated missense/in-frame variants in the catalytic and zinc-binding regions are damaging. Tagged MODEL_ORGANISM because the assay is a whole-organism Drosophila gain-of-function experiment; the same sentence also reports a computational 3D structure analysis, which is not separately curated here.

genes/0.notes: KDM6B (lysine demethylase 6B, also known as JMJD3) encodes a JmjC domain-containing histone H3K27me2/me3 demethylase at 17p13.1. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with the great majority of variants arising de novo; see the disease-level inheritance block.

evidence.snippet: It is highly probable that the complexity of these cases requires an approach by a multidisciplinary team
evidence.explanation: Explicit clinical recommendation for multidisciplinary management of KDM6B-related disease. The quote is trimmed to the last complete word before the cached abstract itself is truncated.

treatments/0.description: No disease-modifying therapy exists. Management is supportive and anticipatory: early intervention with physical, occupational, and speech therapy for developmental delay and hypotonia, educational support for learning difficulties, and coordinated follow-up across genetics, neurology, and psychiatry. Psychiatric surveillance from adolescence is warranted given the reported psychosis risk.

treatments/0/targets/0.description: Supportive care addresses the organism-level developmental and behavioral consequences rather than the underlying chromatin lesion.

evidence.snippet: These findings expand the phenotypic spectrum of this syndrome, highlighting the potential role for KDM6B in cerebellar development and providing valuable insights for genetic counseling.
evidence.explanation: The clinical literature frames phenotype delineation in this disorder as directly serving genetic counseling.

treatments/1.description: Counseling covers the autosomal dominant, predominantly de novo mechanism, the low but non-zero sibling recurrence risk from parental germline mosaicism, the possibility of a mildly affected transmitting parent, and the wide variability of the phenotype. Establishing the molecular diagnosis also resolves the differential with lysosomal storage and overgrowth chromatinopathies.

evidence.snippet: In addition, the mutant mice display markedly increased locomotor activity and impulsivity, two ADHD-like behavioral traits that are ameliorated by methylphenidate treatment.
evidence.explanation: Model-organism evidence of methylphenidate response in Kdm6b haploinsufficiency; tagged INDIRECT because no human treatment study exists for this disorder.

treatments/2.description: Standard ADHD pharmacotherapy is used symptomatically when attention deficit and hyperactivity are impairing. Direct human trial evidence in KDM6B-related NDD is absent; the mechanistic rationale is supported by rescue of hyperactivity and impulsivity by methylphenidate in the heterozygous Kdm6b mouse. This is preclinical support only and must not be read as disease-specific efficacy evidence.

evidence.snippet: Importantly, morpholino oligonucleotide inhibition of a zebrafish UTX homologue resulted in mis-regulation of hox genes and a striking posterior developmental defect
evidence.explanation: Establishes an evolutionarily conserved developmental-patterning role for the KDM6 demethylase family, the premise of this hypothesis.

evidence.snippet: These results suggest that the demethylase activity of Jmjd3, but not that of Utx, affects mouse axial patterning in concert with alterations in Hox gene expression.
evidence.explanation: Mouse evidence that the KDM6B orthologue itself, through its demethylase activity, controls Hox-dependent skeletal patterning; INDIRECT because the model is a homozygous embryo and the human features are heterozygous and mostly craniofacial/distal.

hypotheses/0.description: The coarse facies, mild distal skeletal anomalies, and axial skeletal findings of the minority phenotype are hypothesised to arise from failure of KDM6B-dependent de-repression of HOX and related patterning loci during craniofacial and skeletal development. Supporting evidence is from model organisms (H3K27me3 control of Hox genes; hox mis-regulation and posterior developmental defects after inhibition of the KDM6 paralogue UTX in zebrafish; reduced Hox expression with anterior homeotic transformation of the axial skeleton in demethylase-deficient Jmjd3 mutant mouse embryos). No human KDM6B craniofacial or limb developmental study has tested this directly, and the features are uncommon in the largest cohort.

evidence.snippet: causes precocious neuronal differentiation, and the NSC population fails to become established in the postnatal DG.
evidence.explanation: The precocious-differentiation arm of the paradox.

evidence.snippet: However, KDM6-deficient NPCs exhibit poor proliferation and a failure to differentiate into neurons and glia.
evidence.explanation: The differentiation-block arm of the paradox, in human cells.

open_questions/0.rationale: Human embryonic stem cell-derived progenitors lacking KDM6 enzymes fail to differentiate into neurons and glia, and Jmjd3 deletion in subventricular zone neural stem cells impairs neuronal differentiation. In the hippocampal dentate gyrus, by contrast, Kdm6b deletion causes precocious neuronal differentiation that exhausts the stem cell pool. These are opposite directions of effect on the same cell-fate decision. Plausible reconciliations include regional specialisation (dentate gyrus versus subventricular zone and cortex), developmental timing, differing degrees of KDM6A compensation, or partial versus complete loss of KDM6 activity; the entry currently models both as separate nodes rather than forcing one. A further open strand is whether some of KDM6B's requirement is catalytic-independent, which would mean H3K27me3 demethylase activity alone does not account for the disorder; the abstracts available here do not settle that.

open_questions/1.rationale:
PMID:37196654 is the definitive 85-individual cohort and its tables carry denominators for every recurrent manifestation, including several that this entry curates without a frequency band and at least two that it cannot curate at all. The publisher blocks full-text download, so `just fetch-reference PMID:37196654` yields an abstract-only cache, and PMC10257005 is not fetchable through the current reference sources. Per the project rule that snippets must be exact quotes from the cached reference, those numbers cannot be used here yet, and this entry deliberately leaves the bands off rather than transcribing figures it cannot verify.
Two manifestations are consequently absent from `phenotypes` rather than merely unbanded, because no cacheable source documents them in this disorder: sleep disturbance (recorded only as a bare table row in the PMID:31124279 full text) and macrocephaly or postnatal overgrowth (no narrative statement in any cached source; the founding series reports only individual head-circumference centiles in a table). The overgrowth question matters disproportionately, because it is the phenotypic hinge against the Weaver, Sotos, and Cohen-Gibson differentials that this entry lists: if a substantial minority of KDM6B patients are macrocephalic, the clean "eraser loss gives no overgrowth" contrast drawn in those differentials needs qualifying.

evidence.snippet: Here, by examining the molecular and clinical spectrum of 85 reported individuals with mostly de novo (likely) pathogenic KDM6B variants, we demonstrate that this description is inaccurate and potentially misleading.
evidence.explanation: Direct source of the naming controversy recorded here.

open_questions/2.rationale: The syndrome name derives from a 12-patient ascertainment series. The 85-individual cohort found coarse facies and distal skeletal anomalies to be rare while hypotonia and psychosis are unexpectedly common, and stated explicitly that the OMIM description is inaccurate and potentially misleading. Retaining the name risks misdirecting clinical suspicion away from patients who lack dysmorphism. This entry uses the gene-anchored name while preserving MONDO:0032790 and the OMIM label as synonyms.

open_questions/3.rationale: The neural arm of the mechanism is well supported by human stem cell, mouse, and fly data, but no study has connected KDM6B loss to human craniofacial or limb patterning. The HOX/Polycomb route is inferred from work on the paralogue UTX in zebrafish and from the axial homeotic transformation of demethylase-deficient Jmjd3 mutant mouse embryos; neither addresses human craniofacial or limb development. Whether the dysmorphic minority reflects a distinct variant class, a modifier, or simply ascertainment bias is unknown.

open_questions/4.rationale: Psychosis is one of the most clinically actionable features of this disorder, yet the available published characterisations are qualitative and not obviously concordant: OMIM records psychosis in a small percentage of individuals over age 12, while the largest cohort lists it among features that are unexpectedly common. The cohort denominator for individuals aged 12 or older is small. No frequency band can responsibly be assigned from the retrievable abstracts, so none is asserted on the phenotype record.

evidence.snippet: Here we show the impact of KDM6B mosaic brain knockout on the manifestation of different autistic-like phenotypes including repetitive behaviors, social interaction, and significant cognitive deficits.
evidence.explanation: Illustrates that the available mouse characterisation is brain- and behavior-focused, leaving the dysmorphic arm of the human phenotype unmodelled.

open_questions/5.rationale: The heterozygous and mosaic-brain-knockout mouse models are reported in terms of sociability, memory, hyperactivity, impulsivity, and hippocampal synaptic physiology. The mosaic model is brain-restricted by construction and cannot address craniofacial or limb development at all. Homozygous demethylase-deficient Jmjd3 mutant embryos do show an axial skeletal phenotype (anterior homeotic transformation), but at a dosage that does not match the human heterozygous state, and craniofacial and distal limb morphology of constitutive heterozygotes remains unexamined. Evidence therefore exists in a model system but its fidelity to the dysmorphic component of the human disorder is untested rather than absent, which is the defining situation for a HUMAN_MODEL_MISMATCH rather than a plain knowledge gap.

evidence.snippet:
Overlapping phenotypic features between
KDM6A and KDM6B include prominent ears, abnormal dentition, con-
genital heart disease, feeding difficulties, cryptorchidism, joint hyper-
mobility, developmental delay, hypotonia, and behavioral difficulties.
evidence.explanation: Documents that the mechanistically unexplained visceral and connective-tissue features recur across the paralogous KDM6A (Kabuki syndrome type 2) disorder, the observation motivating this gap. The hyphenated line breaks reproduce the cached PDF text verbatim.

open_questions/6.rationale: These features are documented in affected individuals, but no study connects KDM6B loss to gastrointestinal, cardiac, urogenital, or connective-tissue development, so this entry deliberately draws no causal edge to them. KDM6B is expressed in different tissues during development, and the same feature set recurs in Kabuki syndrome type 2, caused by variants in the paralogous H3K27 demethylase KDM6A, which makes a shared KDM6-dependent developmental origin plausible without demonstrating it. Neonatal feeding difficulty co-occurs with hypotonia in reported patients and may be secondary to it, but the founding series records the two only side by side, without a causal assessment.

evidence.snippet: We found that LRBA colocalized with CTLA4 in endosomal vesicles and that LRBA deficiency or knockdown increased CTLA4 turnover, which resulted in reduced levels of CTLA4 protein in FoxP3(+) regulatory and activated conventional T cells.
evidence.explanation: Demonstrates that LRBA participates in CTLA4 vesicle trafficking and recycling.

steps/0.description: LRBA normally colocalizes with CTLA4 in endosomal vesicles and promotes CTLA4 recycling. Loss of LRBA disrupts this intracellular recycling step in regulatory T cells.

evidence.snippet: We found that LRBA colocalized with CTLA4 in endosomal vesicles and that LRBA deficiency or knockdown increased CTLA4 turnover, which resulted in reduced levels of CTLA4 protein in FoxP3(+) regulatory and activated conventional T cells.
evidence.explanation: Supports increased CTLA4 turnover and lysosomal loss after LRBA deficiency.

steps/1.description: LRBA deficiency increases CTLA4 turnover and routing toward lysosomal degradation, accelerating loss of CTLA4 protein.

evidence.snippet: We found that LRBA colocalized with CTLA4 in endosomal vesicles and that LRBA deficiency or knockdown increased CTLA4 turnover, which resulted in reduced levels of CTLA4 protein in FoxP3(+) regulatory and activated conventional T cells.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports CTLA4 depletion in LRBA-deficient regulatory T cells.

steps/2.description: Accelerated CTLA4 turnover in LRBA deficiency reduces CTLA4 protein abundance in FoxP3-positive regulatory T cells.

evidence.snippet: Although 81% of LRBA-deficient patients had normal T-cell counts, 73% had reduced regulatory T (Treg) cell numbers.
evidence.explanation: Human cohort data shows contraction of the regulatory T-cell compartment in LRBA deficiency.

steps/3.description: Many patients with LRBA deficiency have reduced regulatory T-cell counts, further limiting suppressive immune control.

evidence.snippet: We found that LRBA colocalized with CTLA4 in endosomal vesicles and that LRBA deficiency or knockdown increased CTLA4 turnover, which resulted in reduced levels of CTLA4 protein in FoxP3(+) regulatory and activated conventional T cells.
evidence.explanation: Links CTLA4 depletion to weakened checkpoint-mediated suppression of immune activation.

steps/4.description: Reduced CTLA4-mediated inhibitory signaling weakens checkpoint suppression of immune activation in LRBA deficiency.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with homozygous LRBA mutations had no LRBA, had disturbed B cell development, defective in vitro B cell activation, plasmablast formation, and immunoglobulin secretion, and had low proliferative responses.
evidence.explanation: Directly supports impaired B-cell activation in LRBA-deficient cells.

steps/5.description: LRBA-deficient B cells show a cell-intrinsic activation defect during early effector responses.

evidence.snippet: Most LRBA-deficient patients had low B-cell subset counts, mainly in switched memory B cells (80%) and plasmablasts (92%), with a defective specific antibody response in 67%.
evidence.explanation: Human cohort data confirms reduced switched memory B cells and plasmablasts in LRBA deficiency.

steps/6.description: LRBA deficiency is associated with depletion of switched memory B cells and plasmablasts, indicating defective B-cell maturation and effector differentiation.

evidence.snippet: Individuals with homozygous LRBA mutations had no LRBA, had disturbed B cell development, defective in vitro B cell activation, plasmablast formation, and immunoglobulin secretion, and had low proliferative responses.
evidence.explanation: Establishes defective immunoglobulin secretion in LRBA-deficient B cells.

evidence.snippet: Most LRBA-deficient patients had low B-cell subset counts, mainly in switched memory B cells (80%) and plasmablasts (92%), with a defective specific antibody response in 67%.
evidence.explanation: Cohort data links reduced mature B-cell compartments to defective specific antibody responses.

steps/7.description: LRBA-deficient plasmablasts have impaired immunoglobulin secretion and poor specific antibody responses.

evidence.snippet: Immune dysregulation (95%), organomegaly (86%), recurrent infections (71%), and hypogammaglobulinemia (57%) were the main clinical complications observed in LRBA-deficient patients.
evidence.explanation: Supports hypogammaglobulinemia as a frequent core phenotype in the largest abstract-level cohort.

evidence.snippet: Immune dysregulation (95%), organomegaly (86%), recurrent infections (71%), and hypogammaglobulinemia (57%) were the main clinical complications observed in LRBA-deficient patients.
evidence.explanation: Supports recurrent infections as a frequent major complication of LRBA deficiency.

evidence.snippet: We conclude that mutations in LRBA cause an immune deficiency characterized by defects in B cell activation and autophagy and by susceptibility to apoptosis, all of which are associated with a clinical phenotype of hypogammaglobulinemia and autoimmunity.
evidence.explanation: The discovery paper directly identifies autoimmunity as part of the core clinical phenotype.

evidence.snippet: Most patient had chronic diarrhea (CD) (n:18, 81.8%) and enteropathy was proven by biopsy in 14 (63.6%) patients.
evidence.explanation: Supports chronic diarrhea and enteropathy as very frequent gastrointestinal manifestations.

evidence.snippet: The third common manifestation in LRBA-deficient patients was LP, which was characterized by splenomegaly (n:14, 63.6%), hepatomegaly (n:12, 54,5%) and lymphadenopathy (n: 11, 50%).
evidence.explanation: Supports splenomegaly as a frequent manifestation of LRBA-associated lymphoproliferation.

evidence.snippet: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) and immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) were the most common hematological manifestation and observed in 9 (40.9%) and 11 (50%) patients, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Supports autoimmune hemolytic anemia as a frequent hematologic autoimmune manifestation.

evidence.snippet: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) and immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) were the most common hematological manifestation and observed in 9 (40.9%) and 11 (50%) patients, respectively.
evidence.explanation: Supports immune thrombocytopenia presenting as a frequent thrombocytopenic phenotype in LRBA deficiency.
